Government Orders
Under major investments, in the event that more than 20 per cent of Magna's equity is to be committed to a new, unrelated business, class A and class B shareholders will have the right to approve such an investment with each class voting separately.
Finally, any change to Magna's corporate constitution will require the approval of class A and class B shareholders with each voting separately.
The reason that I took the time to go through every aspect of this corporate constitution is because this bill only deals with one facet of the Canada Post corporate culture. Unless the equity participation program is tied in to the whole philosophy of the post office, then there is absolutely no protection for those people who are buying those shares. There is absolutely no accountability.
This idea, which more and more companies are getting into, is a good idea. It will only work when one considers all aspects of the corporation. One of the members said here earlier that when one deals with a company like Canada Post that in the last few years has shown so little sensitivity in terms of its contribution to the fabric of this country as a whole, then if anything, it is like Canada Post has worked at diminishing the trust factor rather than improving it.
We all know that for many years the Canada postal service was not only a service in terms of the small, rural communities of our country but it was also a symbol of the federal presence. It was one of those instruments of public policy that we used to galvanize and pull this country together.
I can remember 1980 when we would make sure, especially during the referendum, that the presence of the postal service in the province of Quebec was refurbished and rebuilt. We made sure that the flags and the wordmark that became the symbol of the national government were brought up to speed to remind people in the community of the services that this government provides to its citizenry.
I have noticed only in the last few years that on the issue of federal presence-it does not matter what province or community-we have run away from it. First we stripped it of the coat of arms. Now we are stripping it of the Canada wordmark.
In my own riding the two operating post offices, stations A and G, provided services not only for small business people but also for senior citizens. There was staff morale at these centres. These stations were part of the fabric of the community. Now they are closed.
I believe that the postal management has forgotten that one of the key ingredients for having a successful corporation is high morale and a positive spirit. I think the actions that they have undertaken in the last few years are working against that spirit. I cannot quite figure out where management is coming from because the principle behind equity-having your employees own a piece of the company and of the action-is to create a better product and better service at a more competitive price and at a higher level of efficiency.
It seems to me that this is being done in a disjointed way. Assume that this particular bill was to indicate to the current employees of the post office that the shares were not to be bought from their own pockets but, as Magna did, 10 per cent of the shares were to be allocated and distributed to all employees of the post office out of profits. Then there might be a chance of turning the spirit of this postal organization around.
It is human nature that if people are treated fairly, then obviously the productivity levels improve. Here is an opportunity where the postal service has really missed the boat.
I support the position that this will in no way, shape or form enhance the postal service of this country. It will not enhance the spirit or the environment of the people who work in the post office. I take that from all levels, from management to people who work on the line.
I do not think this is a good formula and I would encourage the government to go back to the drawing board. It should take what is basically a good principle and put it in a form where there is accountability. This is not tied together in a comprehensive way.
It should go back to the drawing-board and look at some other successful corporations in this country like Magna, which has been doing very well in the middle of this depression. Its eamings-per-share ratio is topping the charts. Its profits are at record levels. The chief executive officer of that company credits that high level of productivity and morale to the fact that there are close to 17,000 shareholders in the Magna corporation. They
March 9, 1993

know that at the end of the year 10 per cent of that pre-tax profit that will go toward buying shares for distribution among the employees.
This allows a company to make a better product at a better price. Magna is now as competitive as the Germans and the Japanese. This is the kind of comprehensive approach that we need for the basic idea of equity participation and profit sharing for employees. It is a totally above the board approach where everything is in the open. Management is as accountable as the employee. It is not something like this which is only a partial measure.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for the question.

One of our members in the House spoke earlier about some ideas that could be introduced into the postal service. He mentioned banking services and I think that is a good idea.
The problem we have is this government. By the way, it does not matter who the next leader of the party is, it can be the member from Vancouver or the member from Quebec. Essentially what we have on that side of the House is a philosophy that it retreats from national government. It has been the greatest retreat from national governance in the history of our country. If it looks at something and it is not showing an instant viability it cuts it, trashes it and just gets rid of it.
I cannot understand the problem that most business people have. I know there are a few people over there that have business experience, but they obviously do not have any influence on this cabinet. In business when your viability is in jeopardy, creativity comes into the boardroom, into the plant or into all facets of the business. The idea is to say that if we are losing sales and we are not viable, how are we going to diversify? How are we going to get more product into the pipe to make the enterprise more viable so we can keep it alive, so we can keep our people employed?
Government has an added responsibility. It is not just that we have to be concerned with fiscal responsibility and with taxpayers' money, we in governance have to make sure that those regions of our country that do not have the critical mass in terms of population have the same national standards as a person does in a richer centre.
That is part of what being Canadian is all about, having national standards or national services. It does not matter what part of the country you are from, whether you are from a disadvantaged region, rural Canada or downtown Toronto. This government has totally missed the boat on that particular feeling or attitude in the country as a whole.
I see the Minister of Supply and Services here. I know in his department of government there is a lot of good creative Public Service talent. Why could we not take some of these rural post offices and make them centres where we would not only supply some of these banking machines but make them centres where small businesses could come in and maybe bid on government contracts?

They could be mini centres where you would have total government service. With the computer technology that we have today you could make these institutions more than just post offices. Mr. Speaker, I would like to pose an idea to the member for Broadview-Greenwood and invite some comment and perhaps an answer. Part of my comment is really a question.
In my view one of the problems we have had in the Canada Post Corporation in the last while is that the systems analysts and the engineers have taken over. Given the lack of meaningful input from employees or people who work closely with the corporation, particularly in rural Canada but in all ground floor operations in communities across the country, everything has been done to make the corporation fit some self-designed system rather than designing the corporation and procedures within the corporation to fit the needs of the community.
I want to give a couple of examples. The hon. member may not be familiar with my constituency of Kootenay West-Revelstoke, coming from Toronto. To mail a letter from Slocan to New Denver, which is 20 miles away, the letter gets shipped across three valleys, two mountain ranges, a couple of hundred miles to the west to get sorted. In order to come back it returns over the three valleys, two mountain ranges and across a couple of ferries or through an airport where often the planes do not land because of the weather. It takes a week to get 20 miles to another community.
That has been done in order to fit the system that some flaky systems analyst or engineer who is completely out of touch with reality has designed. That sort of thing just does not make sense. If those in responsible positions within the corporation had some continuing dialogue with people who actually experience real life in those kinds of communities, whether through a central agency or some other way-we can work out the mechanism later-maybe they would avoid this kind of bureaucratic nightmare.

Mr. Speaker, I want to go back to my Magna experience. Do you know, minister, it was quite an interesting two years. It would be a good place to consider after the next election. It is creative, it is positive.
The thing which amazed me about Stronach was that when he would inspect plants, he would inspect the garbage cans because that is where you could tell the morale of the troops. If there was waste of raw materials in the garbage cans you knew that the plant was not functioning. In other words, there are too many MBAs today. I have nothing against MBAs, but the unique thing about Magna was that the toolmakers were running the company. They had a couple of token MBAs trying to look after the books, a couple of accountants, but Stronach had this view, this vision, this feeling and it is working out very well.
I really think it is a model that we have to look at. I never agreed with all of Frank's ideas. Some of them were a little far out. The point is that if you have respect for the person who is working on the shop floor, and if you listen to that person, that is where the real creative energy flows. That is how you make better product and provide better service at a competitive price.
There are too many leaders and too many corporations in this country that are like the post office. I say this with respect to the post office, I think it is lacking in that area too. I think it is time to review it and go back to the shop floor and therein will be hope for all of us.

Mr. Speaker, I admit I have mixed feelings about taking part in today's debate. Of course I support my colleagues who are against this bill for a number of reasons. First of all, the bill proposes to sell 10 per cent of the shares to employees without giving them voting rights as shareholders. The tax credit is an excellent proposal, but the bill does not provide for direct participation by employees in the management and operations of Canada Post.
The idea is admirable. We must admit that. However, I would like to share a somewhat personal example with my colleagues in this House, having been actively involved when the employees of Spruce Falls Power & Paper Co. Limited in Kapuskasing, in my riding, acquired a majority interest in their company. For them it was a very significant development, because from that moment on they were in control of their own future and participated directly in the company's management decisions. Their attitude changed dramatically. They took a great deal more pride in their work, absenteeism went down and finally they had a sense of belonging and at the end of the day, when they retired, they would have something very tangible and worthwhile to call their own.
That is not what Bill C-73 does. If the government had intended to at least give these new shareholders voting rights, I would have supported the bill from the word go. Unfortunately that is not the case. And add to that the unsavoury developments of the past 10 years during which we saw a Crown corporation, which in the final analysis belongs to Canadians, gradually edge toward privatization.
There is a price to pay and it was paid by closing down many small post offices. Small, because they are located in Canada's rural areas. It is a very high price because in most cases the post office was the only place in the community that had a federal presence. It was probably the only building flying the Canadian flag.
During the debate around the referendum and the Charlottetown accord, we saw that Canadians still have this very strong desire to feel part of this Canadian
Government Orders
community. Canada Post was one way to promote Canadian unity.
Those of my constituents who went to the post offices have now been closed-six were closed in my riding-felt very strongly about this presence. To them it was a sign that the federal government took them seriously, that they were important. It is something we tend to forget in our large urban centres, in Canada's largest cities, where because of the population density the federal presence is everywhere and all departments are represented.
In small rural post offices there was also the human factor. I have another experience I would like to share with you. My parents, and especially my mother, ran a post office in the small community of Opasatika for 37 years. I remember that when my mother died there were so many people at the funeral that our small church was full. I felt I had to mention my mother's contribution to this community. Every day she met people from the village who came to pick up their mail at the post office. She always had a friendly word for these people and that is why they liked her.
The post office was also a place to meet people, to talk and get the latest news, because we always had a bulletin board where people could put up whatever they wanted. My point is that the kind of personal contact we had before is now gradually disappearing.
We also had the supermailboxes that caused so many problems, especially in rural areas where in the winter snow removal is sometimes less than perfect. I need hardly mention the problems caused by these mailboxes when they are frozen shut. I think this is ample proof that the purpose of the bill is certainly not to improve operations, especially in rural areas.
Last year, another post office in my riding, the one in Moonbeam, was about to close. People rallied to this cause. They wanted to make sure their post office did not close, since the building as such was relatively new, in good condition and the quality of service provided was also very much appreciated by the people in Moonbeam.
We do not know what happened and probably never will, but believe it or not, we managed to keep this post office open. More power to Canada Post, which realized

Government Orders
that the post office was a very important part of the municipality. The question arises now why the same cannot be done for other small communities.
There are minor changes that can be made if Canada Post is losing money. It is not making a profit. And besides, we have to adjust, especially in these difficult times. No one will deny that adjustments and changes are necessary to save money but closing down a post office altogether, especially for the people who appreciate the service, is very difficult to accept. Since Canada Post is aware of this, one wonders why it is pursuing this policy of closing down rural post offices in Canada.
I have another example of service cutbacks. Last week, the post office in Kapuskasing announced that it would be open 16 hours less per week. The important thing is not the number of hours but the principle behind this decision. Let me explain.
First of all, there will be no more mail sorting on Saturday. As a result, on Monday morning letter carriers will have less mail to deliver since it will still be in the bags or on the tables. So one service is being cut. Instead of getting our mail on Monday, as we did for so many years, we will not get it until Thesday.
Second, people were told that in all cases of address changes the mail would be rerouted to Ottawa. It is very hard to make sense of all this because it used to take one hour a day to do address changes, which meant that the mail was delivered the same day. Sending it to Ottawa means it will now take four days for the mail to come back.
What kind of service is this? What is this about paying $110 for a change of address? What about the fact that first-class mail, which normally should be delivered the same day, will now be delivered four days later? I think the reactions of business people are understandable since they feel they are paying quite enough for a service that is very important to them. Consider the reactions of these business people who in future will be more inclined to use the services of private mail courier companies across Canada. If Canada Post thought it could save money this way it was wrong. It was very wrong indeed.
In concluding, I would say that selling these shares to employees might be very beneficial since the same employees would certainly be more inclined to protect the interests of Canada Post. But that is not the case. The current trend is for employees to be far more involved in their company, whether it employs 1, 3, 5, 10 or even 500 people. It is clear that in future the trend will be for employees to participate directly in the operations and decision making of their companies. Since that is not what this bill sets out to do, I see it as my duty to vote against this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for Victoria for his question. No, this bill will not serve to improve employee-employer relations at all.
This is why I was saying in my speech that the actual tendency for employees to participate in their company is not being addressed in Bill C-73. It is not being addressed because the shares that will be sold to those employees are non-voting shares.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak in this debate. I might just ask my friend the member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception if he would

like to speak in the debate before one o'clock, in which case I can try to accommodate him. Is the memeber ready to do that?
Yes.

Fine. I will try to keep my remarks brief in order to do that. This bill has been thoroughly debated in the House. It was debated at second reading. I had a chance to participate there and put some of my views on the record. I should not take too long.
I do want to speak as forcefully as I can against this bill. This bill would really be a first step toward the privatization of Canada Post and perhaps there are cases where privatization may be valid although, coming from the tradition that I do, there are probably fewer occasions than many other members of this House would see. There may be occasions but this is not one of them.
Canada Post has been run as a corporation of the 19th century variety for a long time. That is the source of the problem. The leadership of Canada Post obviously went to the Ebenezer Scrooge school of labour relations. As a result, the labour relations within Canada Post are abysmal.
Instead of using the term labour relations one might almost use the term management relations because the responsibility for the problems of employee relations in Canada Post clearly rests with management. No other management in the country could pile up over 100,000 grievances so that the whole system is in gridlock. It now becomes impossible for an employee who has a legitimate grievance to expect any industrial justice within Canada Post. The system has failed and it is the responsibility of management. This bill does nothing to address that.
There are problems as well in the simple functioning of Canada Post and without consultation with employees. It is a breach of a fundamental rule of modem management. Canada Post persists time and time again to put into practice new methods that are designed to create anxiety within the work force and to slow down efficiency for the general public.
For example, in Victoria it has just recently instituted a system. Instead of sorting the mail in Victoria on a Friday and over the weekend, it takes the mail from Victoria-if one can imagine it-by ferry to Vancouver to run it through the sorting machine on the weekend. It then brings it back on Monday or Tuesday to deliver it a day late to the people of Victoria. It is typical. It is unfortunately typical. The consequences in service are dramatic.
Probably all of us have experienced phoning Canada Post with an inquiry. You cannot talk to any human being in Canada Post any more. You end up having to phone somewhere else. Victoria is a capital city and one of the growing regions of this country, but Canada Post has moved its inquiry service to Vancouver. You end up phoning somebody in Vancouver who usually does not know what part of Victoria you are talking about.
I had an experience just the other day phoning Canada Post. First, I was put on hold but eventually got somebody who said it was not their department. The call was referred to somebody else who also said it was not their department. Again the call was put on hold. Eventually the line died. There was no answer. Thousands of Canadians experience that in seeking to find out what has happened to their mail or their service.
All Canadians have suffered from the junk mail that gets thrown in. When I was looking into one of these problems in my riding, I came across the mentality that now pervades Canada Post. The officials started talking about service to the customer. It turned out they were talking about service to the companies that wanted to get their junk mail into people's homes.
The customer is no longer the general public, the people who wish to mail correspondence and have it delivered in a reasonable period of time. The customer is the corporate sector. It seemed to me that summarized the problems at Canada Post.
We need to change. Instead of the direction in which this bill takes us, we need to change our whole approach to Canada Post. We need to begin with a thorough consultation with the public. I would say that in each area of Canada, Canada Post and the administration should establish small committees of the public to begin looking at the problems at Canada Post from the public's point of view.
This should be joined by a genuine consultation with the employees through their unions to seek changes in Canada Post. If your work force does not have good and

March 9, 1993
Government Orders
high morale you simply cannot deliver the service that you are asked to.
This bill is flawed. It opens the door to the privatization of Canada Post. It fails to deal with the labour relations problems at Canada Post. It makes no effort to change the management at Canada Post. Until the management is changed it is not going to be possible to change the attitudes that pervade Canada Post, the attitudes that are bringing this great service to a standstill.
I call on the House to defeat this bill at this stage. Send this whole mess back to the government with a requirement that it take a completely different approach than it has been taking on services to the public by Canada Post.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I want to thank my hon. friend from Victoria for this opportunty. He and I will be attending the same meeting this afternoon. I do appreciate his consideration in giving me the opportunity to speak on this bill at third reading as this afternoon's activities would have precluded this.
I want to make reference to the comments by my hon. colleagues who have spoken on this subject. My colleague from Essex-Kent spoke eloquently and with great substance on the issue this morning. My hon. colleague from Cochrane-Superior was the most recent speaker on the Liberal side. Of course, there was the hon. member for Victoria who is not to be forgotten. They put a human face on what is happening to Canada Post.
I am vehemently opposed to the bill. If anything needs to be done with Canada Post, it is not to privatize it. It is not to put together a piece of legislation that causes the initial steps to be taken for privatization. These are measures that mitigate and almost put the employees in a different category of persons. The idea is that they would have shares but non-voting shares. I do not want to get into the details of this bill because it has gone through committee and has been discussed.
I think the principle of the bill really calls into question the whole business of how the postal service is run in
Canada. I am going to read something for clarification and for the benefit of putting a certain aspect to my relatively short presentation here this morning.
When the Crown corporation of Canada Post was created under the Canada Post Corporation Act a few years ago, the mandate had five or possibly six principles. I am concerned with the first principle that is described as: "The desirability of improving and extending its products and services''-I underline services-"in the light of the developments of the field of communications".
If some of the examples we have heard in the last 10 minutes in this House are improving the field of communications, one human being communicating with another, then I think we are far off the mark.
The mandate given in 1986 for Canada Post to close 5,221 rural post offices-not urban but rural post offices-at a loss of 10,000 jobs has been well under way. I am told that 1,200 of these post offices have been closed in rural Canada and roughly 3,200 people have lost their jobs. The principle of people losing their jobs when we have 1.6 million Canadians unemployed today is despicable and shameful. The aspect of this in a generic sense is very disturbing.
I will give the most recent example, but for that example there could have been many others and there are many others. I do not fault the officials involved. Officials working for a Crown corporation or for the government have a mandate. They have a job to do and have terms of reference. If they do not do it, they are fired. Who wants to be fired today when the unemployment situation is as it is? If you lose your job you may not qualify for unemployment insurance, thanks to another recent initiative by this government.
I am quoting the example of Spaniard's Bay, a community of about 3,000 people in my riding. Having set a meeting on short notice for December we managed to get it cancelled and delayed until after Christmas. On January 10 representatives of Canada Post met with the elected representatives of Spaniard's Bay. I was unable to attend.
I was told by the political representative, the member of the House of Assembly for that meeting and the follow-up meeting, that every possible objection in the world was raised as to why Spaniard's Bay, which had
March 9, 1993

already had its postal services degraded by the number of hours two years before did not want to have any change made.
Both the officials sat there nodding their heads. All they could do was repeat their mandate that when a natural opportunity arises the postmaster will have to retire and we will have to resort to another kind of postal service. That is what is being done all over Canada. That is what is being done in these 5,221 cases. That is what is going to be done with this community. Why? Because it is done for everybody. No compassion can be shown because it is their mandate.
Imagine the wrath, the ire, the disappointment and the surprise of the people in Spaniard's Bay when they discovered those five recent cases which happen to have been in the Prime Minister's riding. There are others as well. I am not going to quote the details because I do not have time, but five post offices in towns with populations of 363, 3,733, 4,000, 1,000, 225 and in the most blatant case 121. Canada Post advertised that the post office would have an immediate vacancy. Nobody applied for the job. In accordance with its rule it should have closed it down anyway because of the natural opportunity but it did not and went out again to hire somebody else. This is not applying the rules and the mandate in a fair and balanced manner.
One example of why I believe that if we need anything to improve Canada Post and if we have any bills and legislation to be passed in this House it should be to go back and restore to Canadians the proper service that the Prime Minister promised in an election promise in 1984 when he said that improving the service of Canada Post is going to be a top priority for the government.
If closing down 5,221 post offices in rural Canada is another blow of the demolition derby of this government of destroying rural Canada then I do not see that as an improvement in service. I would certainly say that if this is used in substantiation of trust in the government to approve Bill C-73 on third reading then I think it has gone about it in the wrong way and it is far from receiving the support from this side of the House and many of my colleagues.

speechtext:

AFTER RECESS

Mr. Speaker, the governments concerned should thoroughly investigate the effects of tobacco smuggling. This is urgent. Merchants find that cigarette smuggling is making life difficult for them. The tax system must be re-evaluated and some Indian reserves and other networks that benefit from this smuggling, which deprives the governments of hundreds of millions of dollars, must be brought into line.
We should recover these amounts by lowering the taxes of the various levels of government. Will we tolerate this flagrant lawlessness for long? I call on the ministers of finance, revenue and justice of the governments concerned to take the bull by the horns and lay down the law for those who traffic illegally in cigarettes and alcohol and evade taxes.
Does the will exist to eliminate this scourge from Quebec and Canada?

Mr. Speaker, ludicrous, stupid and destructive are just a few of the adjectives that have been used to describe this government's latest round of cuts to Official Development Assistance.
Those of us who have committed our lives to ensuring that the people most in need are the beneficiaries of Canadian aid are flabbergasted at the changed policy directions being implemented by this government, changes

March 9, 1993
which represent the abandonment of our stated official policy to help the poorest countries and people in the world.
The changed policy direction implemented because of a 10 per cent cut to our aid budget has been implemented without benefit of public consultation and in an election year when the government's mandate has run out.
Mr. Mahbub ul Haq, the author of the UNDP report, suggested that a move in this direction "would be an unmitigated disaster". Not only were these cuts implemented without Canadian public consultation but they were also implemented without consultation with the affected countries.
Just as this government has shown through its policies that it has little regard for the people of this country, it is with these measures demonstrating its lack of regard for the poorest people in the world. This government obviously does not comprehend the nature of development assistance and the need for a people first, grass roots development policy which will lift civil societies to self-determination and self-sufficiency.

Mr. Speaker, Taqra-miut Nipingat is concerned about the budget cuts announced on December 2 for native communities' communications programs.
This organization produces radio and television programs by Inuit people in Inuktitut and distributes them in northern Quebec. As well as preserving Inuit culture and protecting their language, Taqramiut Nipingat provides essential communication services for thousands of people.
I sincerely believe that this communication program must not be cut back, given the economic importance of northern Quebec and this remote region.
I ask the Minister of Finance to revise Bill C-113, because Taqramiut Nipingat is one of the few opportunities for training and employment in the North.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians have been shocked by recent news stories about the epidemic of suicide among aboriginal young people. Studies show that aboriginal youth are killing themselves at rates five to seven times that of the national average.
In Big Cove, Davis Inlet, the Nishnawbe-Aski communities in northwestern Ontario, and Stanley Mission in my riding the story is the same. Unemployment rates of 80 to 90 per cent and centuries of cultural genocide are the reasons these young people are giving up hope.
Yet this year the federal government has cut economic development programs for aboriginal people by over $40 million while it has increased welfare budgets by $52 million. Excellent proposals for coming to terms with this issue are coming in from First Nations across the country, but they are caught on the bureaucratic treadmill while the crisis in their community accelerates.
Our First Nations people want to end the cycle of dependency and despair. Canadians overwhelmingly share their vision of a future with hope for aboriginal youth.
It is only this government, which has the primary responsibility for aboriginal people, that is not getting the message. Until it does young people are going to pay the price.

Mr. Speaker, concerned citizens around the world were shocked by the recent murder of a two-year old in Britain by two 10-year old boys. Unfortunately the same attitude that fostered that crime also exists in Canada today.
People from coast to coast are demanding action to stop the increasing violence in our society. It is necessary

March 9, 1993

for all levels of government to work together in an effort to determine the causes of such attitudes and behaviours and to institute remedies for these problems.
It is indeed difficult to legislate morality and good behaviour, but for the sake of our country and future generations every effort must be made now in many areas to restore safety to our streets.
Some areas of concern include the increasing violence on television and in films, pornography, the breakdown of the family, over-emphasis on rights while ignoring responsibilities, poverty, and the lack of adequate facilities to assist disturbed youth. I ask all governments and society to work together to combat this alarming trend.

Mr. Speaker, the lack of a coherent transportation policy in Canada is nowhere more evident than in northern Ontario. By cancelling VIA Rail in the north and by its failure to act on western grain transportation this government has clearly demonstrated that it lacks the will and the courage to make the necessary changes to treat east and west fairly in Canada.
This government is driving regions toward north-south orientation. They must do this for their economic future. Look at Sault Ste. Marie, linked to the best interstate system in the world, and Windsor and southwestern Ontario and its proximity to Michigan. Sarnia is only the width of a river from the interstate system. In my own area of northwestern Ontario we will be forced into a north-south transportation network. We are 40 miles away from this interstate system.
I wonder how long it will take the people in Canada in those regions to go to Amtrak to look after their passenger rail service? This government's transportation policy is forcing regions to protect their economic future in a way that is not in Canada's best national interest. They are going north and south rather than east and west.

Mr. Speaker, on February 2 in the House I made a statement and
asked the Minister of Agriculture about the proposed changes to the Feed Freight Assistance Program. If the changes are approved as proposed they will penalize Atlantic Canadian farmers unduly and unfairly.
Another proposed change that will harm Atlantic Canada will be the reduction in the maritime freight rate program which assists Atlantic Canadian industry in being competitive. This program has been in place since 1927.
If these long-standing programs are reduced as proposed Atlantic Canada will lose its ability to compete. Both the agricultural and industrial communities have proposals before their respective departments. These plans address the financial needs of the government but do not place an undue burden on Atlantic Canada.
In the interest of government and business working together in Atlantic Canada I ask the ministers involved to implement the proposals submitted instead of the plans presently on the table.

Mr. Speaker, I repeatedly called for an environmental assessment review panel for the proposed additions to runways at Pearson International Airport.
I am dismayed by Transport Canada's decision to disregard the panel's recommendations. The panel's report states that no decision should be taken at this time with regard to the construction of one or more additional runways at Pearson.
Further, the report rightly observes that any decision to proceed will be perceived as a signal that the concerns expressed before the panel, like previous efforts to mitigate the adverse social impacts at Pearson, have fallen on deaf ears.
There are major implications for public policy in Transport Canada's decision to ignore its own environmental assessment panel. Whatever the actual conclusions of the panel, the government's decision simply to overrule its recommendations raises fundamental questions about the efficacy of all such reviews, not to mention the futile expenditure of taxpayers' money.

March 9, 1993
The residents of Etobicoke and other communities urge the government to reverse its decision and develop a total transportation strategy which alleviates rather than exacerbates the already formidable environmental burdens placed on the communities surrounding Pearson International Airport.

Mr. Speaker, it was with shock and horror that I heard the hon. member from Mississauga refer to the subcommittee on poverty as a kangaroo committee.
In doing so she maligned not only the chair but every member of that committee and members sitting on all sides of this House. Her remarks are outrageous.
Has she not heard of the Brighter Futures initiative? Does $2.6 billion mean nothing to her? What about the child tax benefit designed to help low income families? Was the member not paying attention?
It is tragic that any Canadian citizen must live in poverty. The plight of Canadian children is one of great concern to us all. The Liberals and the NDP do not hold a monopoly on compassion. This government has worked hard, not only to provide financial support to disadvantaged Canadians but, more important, to provide them with the tools to become self-reliant.
Perhaps it is time my colleague was apprised of this government's achievements in the area of social-
The members' time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, last week the government signed an agreement to sell uranium to Taiwan in breach of the spirit of the nuclear non-proliferation treaty. Until now, Canada has always insisted that Canadian nuclear materials would be sold only to signatories to the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, which is designed to stop the spread of nuclear weapons.
This treaty is up for renewal in 1995 and faces a very difficult round of negotiations. Canada and the world have a tremendous stake in the success of these negotiations yet the government is undermining the treaty on the eve of the renewal negotiations, contrary to the security of Canadians and the peoples of the world.
To make it worse, the government is routing the sale through the United States to avoid the terms of the treaty and it entered into the agreement after the Minister of Agriculture visited Taiwan, in another breach of official Canadian policy.

Mr. Speaker, aboriginal communities throughout the country are in desperate need. Aboriginal people know what must be done but this government continues to deny them the tools they need to work with.
A vicious cycle links poverty and inadequate and overcrowded housing to family violence, substance abuse and suicide. Yet this government has done nothing to improve aboriginal and northern housing and economic conditions. In fact, this government has made matters worse.
Despite an aboriginal and northern housing crisis, aboriginal and northern housing funds have been cut. Despite high aboriginal unemployment rates, aboriginal economic development and aboriginal communications funds have been cut.
In northern Canada aboriginal language television provides jobs and information on social issues that people cannot get otherwise due to their remoteness.
A new approach is needed which realizes that all things are connected and solutions will come from the people themselves if they are given the opportunities. This government has failed to provide these opportunities. It is time for a new government.

Mr. Speaker, in Saskatchewan we have recently experienced the Saskatchewan NDP supporting enhanced trade with Mexico. There has been a weak attempt by the Saskatchewan NDP to say: "Yes, but".
A recent article in The Regina Leader Post states: NAFTA bashing by NDP becoming a little tiring.
March 9, 1993

It highlighted this back-and-forth posturing.
I would entreat eveiyone who truly cares to know more about this trading relationship to read this article. It concludes by saying, and I quote again:
In sum, the NDP/trade union position on free trade is a collection of worn-out cliches that presents the facade of solidarity, while attempting to conceal political hypocrisy and union self-interest.
It is time for all parties to recognize that Canada's economic growth and the maintenance of our standard of living are interconnected. Both should be above partisanship.

Mr. Speaker, the decision of the Ontario Provincial Police not to charge Ernst Zundel for promoting hatred and lies about the holocaust is extremely disappointing.

The decision to lay criminal charges under the hate crime provision of the Criminal Code rests with the NDP Attorney General, Marion Boyd. Instead of recognizing the fact that holocaust denial is one of the most powerful weapons of the neo-Nazi movement the provincial NDP in Ontario is burying its head in the sand.
The German government has complained that materials published by Zundel in Canada are being used to fuel the rise of Nazi and extreme right-wing racist organizations. It is time to put an end to this kind of criminal activity.
I hope that the provincial NDP government uses the power it does have to put an end to this type of hate propaganda.

Mr. Speaker, in Canada we have a lot to learn. International tests have been done in math and science. Canadian students in grade four perform at the international average, but by grade eight they are out-performed by students in many other countries.
Canadian high school graduates have even poorer results. Testing of basic skills over the past 25 years shows deteriorating achievements. Somewhere along the line we are letting our students down.
In late 1991 provinces recognized the need for national standardized testing, but the proposed school achievement indicators program ran into problems along the way.
As a nation we want our graduates to be competitive in the new global economy. We want our students to stay in school, to learn, to achieve and to move into challenging jobs. I hope we will work as a nation toward achieving these goals.
Governments at all levels can put together a system of standardized testing that will help parents and educators to identify and meet the needs of our students throughout their education.

Mr. Speaker, this government is in an utter state of confusion over its position on the NAFTA legislation and the proposed parallel accords on the environment and labour standards.
The Prime Minister says that perhaps the legislation should be delayed, and in reference to the accords he says: "They have little if anything to do with Canada".
On the other hand the trade minister says they will ram the NAFTA through before July 1 and then again contradicts the Prime Minister by saying that the accords are important to Canada and that we must be at the table.
Meanwhile the finance minister demonstrates similar confusion on the domestic front. He promises a budget some time soon to present a plan to deal with the deficit. This plan, he says: "will probably be based on the previous plan we had which has slipped".
What we have is a new plan based on a failed old plan. It is obvious this government is in a total state of confusion. It has no leader, no direction domestically and obviously no direction internationally.

March 9, 1993
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister of defence.
An internationally recognized aviation magazine has reported that Agusta, the Italian company from which the government is buying the EH-101 helicopters, is now $1.4 billion in the red and is now under the bankruptcy protection rules in Italy.
The Italian government appears both unwilling and unable to provide a bailout under the European Community rules.
Why is the minister insisting on risking billions of dollars of taxpayers' money to support a company that is about to collapse? Will she not at least suspend the contract so that we can ascertain that Canadians will not end up subsidizing a bankrupt foreign company?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the government has no reason to believe that the contract will not be performed as stipulated.

Mr. Speaker, let me ask a supplementary question about how this performance will be completed.
In late January the EH-101 prototype helicopter crashed for unknown reasons, killing four people including the test pilot. The Italian ministry of transport has grounded the eight remaining prototypes and has opened an inquiry which has yet to report.
Why has the government made the commitment to buy an expensive piece of equipment which has not yet proven to be either safe or reliable? How much will this government pay for somebody else's mistakes?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the prototype to which the hon. member refers that did crash is not the same model that is the subject of our contracts.
The government has chosen this model to replace the two fleets of helicopters and the fleet of fixed-wing aircraft for the same reason that the member of that
hon. member's party who sat on the standing committee supported unanimously with his colleagues the purchase of these helicopters in November 1990.

Mr. Speaker, the minister knows full well that when that committee reported the cost of the helicopters was less than 40 per cent of what it is now, before the collapse and crash of the prototype.
In sum, the minister is telling us that the government has committed billions of dollars to buy helicopters it has yet to prove it can fly in a safe and reliable fashion from a company that is going bankrupt, without any protection for the Canadian taxpayer.
Can the minister tell us what guarantees the government has received on non-performance of this arrangement? In the name of honesty, fairness and good government, will the minister table the helicopter contract so there can be an appraisal of just what commitments are made and how the Canadian government can extract itself from the mess this minister has got us into?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has no basis on which to make the claims he is making.
With respect to the crash of the prototype helicopter, which is in fact not the model that is the subject of our contracts, I am more concerned about the more recent crash of one of our aging Sea Kings off Florida.
I think Canadians want a standard of safety in modem technology and do not wish to play politics with the safety of the men and women who serve in our Armed Forces.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the minister of defence.
The minister of defence and the government continue to ratchet up almost monthly the cost of these helicopters. Originally a number of years ago they were announced at $2 billion. That figure subsequently became $4.4 billion. They acknowledged a few weeks ago that it was $5.8 billion.
March 9, 1993

In the original news communique put out by the minister's predecessor the cost then announced at $4.4 billion included the helicopters, spare parts, technical manuals, training and administrative costs. Not included of course was the cost of arms for those helicopters and the cost of strengthening frigates.
I want the minister of defence, because surely she has those numbers at her fingertips, to tell this House, and through this House Canadians, what are the additional costs above known costs to bring these helicopters on stream, to prop up a bankrupt Italian firm and to waste taxpayers' money.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Dick (Minister of Supply and Services):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the numbers that have been used in this House by opposition members, are being used footloose and fancy-free. They are dreaming up numbers almost on a daily basis.
From the time of the announcement the price of these helicopters was $4.4 billion. It is $4.4 billion in today's dollars. It has been from the beginning and will be to the end.
The figure they have then used is what is used in every large contract which goes over 13 years, a figure which is in possible inflated dollars for contingencies in case there is inflation. They try to use that as 2 it is a different figure.
It is $4.4 billion in today's dollars and always has remained the same figure.

Mr. Speaker, that answer is as bankrupt as one of the partners in the joint venture building the helicopters.
I want to ask the minister of defence a question. It is not a supply and services question; it is a defence question. In the fact sheet put out by the minister's department on these helicopters, describing the equipment the helicopters use it describes two torpedoes per helicopter, 24 sonar buoys, smoke markers and so on. That equipment is not included in the press release put out by the department of defence outlining the cost of the helicopters. That is a fact.
What is the additional cost of strengthening 16 frigates? What is the additional cost of purchasing and supplying arms for the 35 helicopters that are deemed to be appropriate to be armed?
Oral Questions
Mr. Minister you haven't told Canadians the full truth. Tell them now.
Oh, oh.

Hon. members on both sides of the House know that it has been our custom and tradition not to use the personal you, no matter how strong one feels about an exchange, and to put the questions through the Speaker.
I would just have to let all hon. members on both sides of the House know I am going to insist on it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Dick (Minister of Supply and Services):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the very first time this issue was brought up I told the hon. member that the cost of the aeroplanes and the systems that were going into them was $1.4 billion plus $1.4 billion for $2.8 billions.
The other costs include the logistics, the spare parts and the other peripheral equipment that goes onto it rather than just the body of the aircraft itself and the systems going into it.
At that time I offered the hon. member, if he wanted, a briefing on this. As a matter of fact he did not go to the briefing until after it closed down. He was not there for the briefing. He was only there for questions that he posed afterward. Only one other member of his party was there for the briefing. He ignored it. He did not want to know the facts.
Oh, oh.
Hear, hear.
We would be very happy for this to come up-
Mr. Speaker, on your feet. That's a lie.
Oh, oh.
The hon. member will retract that statement. The hon. member is not going to get away with that and he knows it.
Withdraw.

I am sure all hon. members would understand that the position of the Speaker is not easy in a situation like this one.
It probably is best, as the hon. member is a very experienced member in this House and has been here for a long time, if perhaps the matter could be settled

March 9, 1993
Oral Questions
between myself and the hon. member. It does not need a lot of comment from everybody else.
Out of respect for the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I withdraw the comment directed at the Chair.
I thank the hon. member. I also thank other hon. members for accepting my suggestion that in a case like this it is best if it is settled by the Speaker and the member who is involved.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate your intervention. This is in fact a very serious issue for all sides of the House. I did attend the briefing. Last fall I asked the associate minister for national defence and she acknowledged that these helicopters did not fit on the frigates and required millions of dollars worth of modification.
It has now been brought to my attention that there are even more serious design problems affecting the working relationship between the helicopters and the frigates, problems which go to the very fundamentals of this project and may require its cancellation.
My question for the minister is a very serious one. Has she been informed of any other design problems affecting the capability of the frigates if they have these helicopters attached to them and, if so, will she inform the House?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I would be pleased to inform the minister that tomorrow details of this will be made public.
Let me simply say that yesterday the minister said to the House that the whole project including the frigates and the helicopters should be reviewed. Those were her precise words. The minister inherited this project from previous ministers.
Will the minister who has gainfully defended this project now show some political courage and set up an independent review of this project and save the Canadian taxpayers billions of dollars in wasted money?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not say I was going to take a review. I simply reminded hon. members that the shipboard helicopters are a completion of the frigate project and if one is going to talk about
cutting them back then that has implications for the frigate project.
When I mentioned the possibility of reviewing that there were heads shaking on the other side of the House clearly not in support of that.
I might say that on taking over as Minister of National Defence of course I reviewed the policies to which we are committed. In reviewing the helicopter project I was much comforted by the support of the hon. member for Victoria who as a member of the standing committee was part of the consensus that supported replacing our Sea King helicopters with the EH-101, and I thank him for that advice.

Mr. Speaker, I quote the minister from Hansard yesterday:
I think this is something that we should review.
I may also make two points to the minister. First, the recommendation was not to purchase the EH-lOls but was instead to replace the Sea Kings. The report did comment favourably on the EH-lOls but times have changed since this report was filed. We on this side are prepared to cancel this agreement in light of the facts that are now in front of us.
Will the minister not face up to the new facts that are coming in daily on this helicopter and will she not agree that it is important to review this purchase and in fact to put it on hold?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would agree with the hon. member that times have changed since November 1990 after the fall of the Berlin wall and the end of the cold war. That hon. member gave his support to this particular project.
I would suggest that what has changed is less the question of the cold war than a more imminent contest which will probably be hotter and which I think is more the motivation of that hon. member's question.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of National Defence.
It is true that the situation has changed and that the Italian company in question is nearly bankrupt. It is also true that the prototype helicopter which she recommends had an accident that killed four people. Since this
March 9, 1993

project was announced last year, the cost has risen not just by $2 billion but possibly by $4 billion now.
So I would like to ask the minister this: Since thousands of children in Canada have no food, would she be prepared to cancel this contract for the sake of Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, what concerns me is the recent accident of one of our old Sea Kings. I am aware that the men and women serving in our Canadian forces need to be safe and not made to fly in old, unsafe helicopters.
Mr. Speaker, if the minister is interested in the women and men in the Armed Forces, why does she want to buy a helicopter of which a prototype had an accident that killed four people?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is not the same prototype as our helicopter. I think it must be pointed out that many prototypes of helicopters and other aircraft in the world have accidents when they are being tested out. This is not a reason to cancel this contract.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of National Defence.
The minister now knows she was wrong yesterday when she told the House that she had not been made aware of outrageous sexist comments made by one of her senior officers. Given that the commandant of the National Defence Medical Centre obviously opposes the government's policy on equality for women in the Armed Forces as stated by the minister in the House yesterday, why has the minister not relieved Colonel G. D. McLean of his duties?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased that the hon. member has raised this question again. On inquiring about the very serious issue she raised, I was advised that the reason why I was not personally aware of it was that it had been resolved. The booth relating to pay equity in the Armed Forces was in
Oral Questions
fact put in place. The member of the Armed Forces who appeared not to understand the policy was dealt with through the appropriate channels.
That issue was resolved before the hon. member raised the question. I am sure she did not know it when she raised the question but I am sure she will be pleased to know there was a satisfactory resolution of it.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.
While the minister is out campaigning she may believe that the issue has been satisfactorily resolved but if she would take off her blue coloured glasses for a moment she would know that jobs performed primarily by women in the Armed Forces are paid at a discriminatory rate compared to jobs performed primarily by men.
If the minister is taking no action concerning Colonel McLean's comments, what specific concrete action will she take today to end pay discrimination against women in her department?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am happy to say that action has already been taken by the Government of Canada. It is the policy of the Government of Canada. It is the policy of the forces of Canada and it is the policy that is being applied in the Canadian Armed Forces.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport.
As the minister knows, the rail industry in Canada is in a crisis. CN is getting rid of its main line from Truro to Sydney. CP is getting out of Atlantic Canada altogether. The two rail companies have merged in the Ottawa valley and are now talking about a full merger east of Winnipeg. Last week CN announced 10,000 more jobs will be cut.
All of this is happening in the absence of any national plan by the federal government to determine what the rail infrastructure should look like.

Oral Questions
My question for the Minister of Transport is this. Will he immediately assign a task force the responsibility of determining what the basic rail infrastructure should be? As part of that, will he impose a moratorium on any main line rail abandonments and any further job cuts until that plan is in place?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member certainly knows, because he was at the press conference this morning, that the NTA review commission has tabled its report. I officially tabled it in the House this morning.
As a result of the tabling of this report I indicated that it would be submitted to the standing committee of the House of Commons for examination and report. At the same time, the Ministry of Transport will be striking a work force to examine both the Royal Commission on passenger transportation and the report of this review commission.

I have a supplementary, Mr. Speaker.
Perhaps the minister should have listened to the question instead of reading the script he was given. I did not ask about the NTA review. I asked about the future of rail in this country. The best thing that the NTA review can come up with is more deregulation, giving the railroads more power to rip up tracks from one end of this country to another.
I want to put my question to the minister again. Will he impose a moratorium on any further main line rail abandonments? Will he impose a moratorium on the job cuts that CN and CP are conducting until we know what kind of rail system we need in this country?

Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member is really interested in the future of the railway he should applaud that CN is being fiscally responsible and has as its objective to properly serve its customers. It has decided to rationalize itself.
The member should know, and I am telling him if he does not know, that the largest railway in the U.S. has a volume of about $5 billion a year and has 31,000 employees. CN has a volume of less than $3 billion and
also has 31,000 employees. It is natural that CN wants to cut, rationalize and become more productive.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the same minister. The report of the National Transportation Act review commission also says that the railroads are in worse shape and risk facing a drastic situation by the end of the decade. The commission also adds in its report that the government should privatize Canadian National. The minister has had this report since January 30. CN employees have a right to know what is going on. Why did the government adopt the policy of privatizing CN Rail?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to know what this member's policy is and what the policy of his party is on this question. This morning, at his own press conference after the tabling of the NTA report, he said he and his party do not fundamentally and forever oppose privatization.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the minister would try answering questions directly and honestly for a change and we might actually have a debate in this House.

I do not think anybody would be too perplexed around here whether anyone on either side of the House wanted either a direct question or a direct response, but I think we can refrain from using the word "honestly" with the imputation that perhaps it is not being given honestly. The hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, I will not use the reference to honest in connection with the minister.
The issue of airlines is also raised in the report. The minister has been saying for some time now that he intends to recalibrate, to use his jargon, the regulatory framework within which the airlines in Canada operate.
His commission's report has not given him any help on that. It is time for the minister to stop waiting for royal commissions, review committees, task forces, transport committees and start answering questions about how he is going to preserve competition on Canadian domestic air service routes in this country.
March 9, 1993

Oral Questions
How is he going to do it? When is he going to do it? When is he going to take responsibility?

Mr. Speaker, my honest answer is that the management of both airlines have recently testified in court that they know what their problem is. It is over-capacity.
If they know what the problem is, then they should attack it themselves. If they do not, then we will intervene.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport.
The minister will note that in the report on the National Transportation Act the commission recommended the removal of regional development as one of the priorities of our national transportation system. He will also know that under great pressure his government was forced to include it in the original 1987 act.
Regional development is absolutely a key component in the transportation systems for all parts of the country. Yet not only when this recommendation came down, but when the royal commission recommendation came down, the minister remained absolutely silent.
Will the minister reassure the House and all Canadians that regional development will remain an effective component of our transportation policy?

Mr. Speaker, the two commissions of inquiry, the Royal commission on passenger transportation and the National Transportation Act review commission, made similar recommendations. Both commissions have transportation experts who devoted a lot of effort to this question.
I think the member should be glad that we will give members an opportunity on the Standing Committee on Transport to examine these recommendations from experts and to provide the Minister of Transport with their own recommendations. At the same time, the Department of Transport will also do its homework to see what recommendations apply, which ones we should accept and which we should not.

Mr. Speaker, my supplemental is for the same minister.
Some of the issues raised in this report are immediately and obviously incorrect. The one dealing with regional development affects not only cities like Winnipeg and Halifax, but Montreal, Quebec City and Baie Comeau. Regional development is key to these cities. By referring it to study and putting it on the back burner, the minister again puts the stability of these local economies at risk.
I ask again: Will the minister reassure the House that this government appreciates the importance of transportation in the regional economies of this country?

Mr. Speaker, I repeat again that these two commissions were composed of specialists in transportation industries. They have made recommendations for the short term, the medium term and the long term.
The hon. member should be very pleased that we are now going to ask members of Parliament to examine this in the Standing Committee on Transport and report to this House on a proper way to handle these recommendations.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Public Works.
As the minister knows, since August 1989 Mr. Alan Scales has been chairman of the federal Crown corporation, Marine Atlantic, which operates the ferry service from Prince Edward Island to the mainland, a service that will be eliminated to pay for the fixed link.
Is the minister aware that Mr. Alan Scales' law firm has been associated with the proponent of the fixed link Strait Crossing Inc. since May of 1988 and that Mr. Scales has now joined in the Federal Court trial to support the Liberal Government of P.E.I. on the side of the fixed link?
What will the minister do about this textbook case of conflict of interest where during part of the day Mr. Scales wears a paediatrician's gown and the rest of the day wears an undertaker's hat?

March 9, 1993
Oral Questions

Will the minister explain to Canadians why as the Minister of Transport he employs Mr. Alan Scales as chairman of the federal Crown corporation Marine Atlantic when the same Mr. Alan Scales is before the Federal Court supporting the Liberal government of Prince Edward Island in its push to kill that same ferry service?
