Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
The good news is that the Self-Employment Incentive Program is working very well in northern Nova Scotia, but the bad news is there is one area that is excluded. That is Colchester county.
Will the minister move to extend the application of SEI to Colchester county and give the people there the same opportunities that everybody else around Colchester has?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fact is that under that option of the Canadian Jobs Strategy, I believe $6.9 million is allocated to Nova Scotia.
As the hon. member knows, because of his good work in his riding of Colchester that area is doing very well. There are other places in much greater need. Unfortunately the criteria is such that we have to take care of those parts of Nova Scotia having a greater need. We are piloting some projects in the Halifax region. I will check as to whether or not we could not pilot this good initiative in the member's riding.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister for International Trade. I believe that he is out for a few minutes, so I will direct it to the Minister of Finance.
The minister has said clearly on several occasions that he would begin negotiations about how to obtain additional guarantees for strengthening the North American Free Trade Agreement in the areas of the environment and labour standards. However, so far, he has refused to promise clearly that the main treaty will not be signed until these supplementary negotiations are concluded. This is extremely important and I believe that the people are entitled to know where the government stands on this question.
Can the minister finally tell us if he will make signing one agreement conditional on signing the other?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first let me say to my hon. friend that the government is quite satisfied that the NAFTA agreement itself is in the interests of Canada and should proceed.
In regard to a side agreement on the environment or labour, we were prepared to discuss these matters with the Americans as long ago as February of last year. I put forward proposals, for side agreements on labour and the environment with both the Americans and the Mexicans. These were turned down.
The Americans have now raised the point again. We are delighted to have an opportunity to put our case forward at this time.

Mr. Speaker, this is a good example of an indirect answer to a very direct question.
No one will understand the refusal of the minister to commit himself on such an important question for all Canadians, especially when President Clinton has just said in a recent speech delivered to an American university and I quote: "That agreement holds the potential to create many jobs in America over the next decade if"-and that is a big if-"it is joined with others
March 9, 1993

to ensure that the environment, living standards, and working conditions are honoured".
Will we see the Americans withholding their signature while this government rushes to the table to sign the main treaty before the conclusion of the parallel agreements? Will this government undermine the American efforts to protect our own environment and our own jobs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, let me say to my hon. friend that the treaty has been signed. The NAFTA agreement was signed last December. It is now up to Parliament and the congresses in Mexico and the United States to pass it.
The Americans have made a statement that they will not pass this unless their Congress approves the side agreements. It has nothing to do with Canada and Mexico. We will participate in that negotiation as well in order to get the best possible terms on the environment and on labour standards.
I should also point out to my hon. friend that there is nothing in the NAFTA itself that allows any other country to impose lower environmental standards on Canada or another country. Indeed, the result of the agreement will be an improvement in the environmental standards in all three countries.

Mr. Speaker, General Motors has announced it is going to lay off an additional 8,675 workers by 1994. These are workers in Oshawa, Scarborough, St. Catharines and Windsor.
In light of these lay-offs I ask the industry minister exactly what conversations he has had with George Peapples, the president of General Motors Canada and exactly what he is going to do about it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I met with Mr. Peapples two and a half weeks ago.
We discussed this in the context of the over-all problems that General Motors is having on a world-wide
Oral Questions
basis. I expressed my deep concern about what is happening to General Motors Canada. He promised that he would take into account these concerns as these decisions are being made.
Let me just point out to my hon. friend that he is referring only to the lay-offs. He has not made any reference at all to the increase in truck production at the plant in Oshawa.

Mr. Speaker, if the minister wants to look at his record in terms of the auto industry, over the past four years Canada has lost 15 per cent of its auto jobs. The United States during the same period has lost only 8 per cent.
If the minister is so proud of his record, can he explain why under his stewardship Canada is losing auto jobs at twice the rate of the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if my hon. friend would go back to 10 years ago and see the proportion of automotive production in Canada relative to our sales in Canada and compare that to the United States, he will see that the result has been a significant increase in jobs in the auto sector.
There has been a considerable increase in production so that today Canada has I believe 17.5 per cent or 18 per cent of the total production in the United States and Canada, compared to the size of the sales market which is about 9 per cent. That is a very good record.

Mr. Speaker, despite our recognition yesterday in this House of International Women's Day, I have a question for the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
There are three women in London, Ontario who are still waiting for this government to recognize gender persecution as a legitimate refugee claim. In fact, Mrs. Simret, Mrs. Sighed and Mrs. Bahlebi-Tcdia are all single mothers fighting deportation to Ethiopia. In three days Mrs. Bahlebi and her son will be deported to a country where she was beaten publicly and persecuted. She has not lived there for over 17 years.

March 9, 1993
Oral Questions
What will the minister and this government do to end the gender discrimination of refugees and introduce a consistent policy which will allow these women and others to stay in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member will be pleased to know that today the chairperson of the Immigration and Refugee Board, Madam Mawani, has issued guidelines on gender-based persecution.
Members of the board will now assess the particular circumstances which have given rise to the claimant's fear of persecution. They will also assess the conditions in the country of origin before entering their decision.
These guidelines are intended to ensure a thorough and sensitive method in this difficult and complex matter. They will promote consistency across Canada and coherence in those decisions rendered on refugee claimants.
The hon. member will also want to know that in January I asked the department to start discussions and consultations with interested persons and groups across Canada so that as a country we can deal with this crucial and important question. That process will take place.
A former member of this House, Mr. Broadbent, has qualified this development as positive and I intend to pursue it.

Mr. Speaker, in some circumstances the minister of immigration does not need any guidelines. He can glean advice from another government ministry.
A Russian woman in my riding, Irina Aoucheva, and her Canadian-born daughter face imminent deportation if the minister fails to intervene. While immigration officials say that Irina's claim of persecution is unfounded, experts at external affairs tell me that: "The situation is so confused in Russia that there are no guarantees for their safety one way or the other". In fact, while immigration officials go by the book, external affairs advises: "Russian law is not at the state where local authorities could prevent anything from happening to this woman".
Why is the minister refusing to accept this advice? Is he prepared to submit this woman and her Canadian bom baby to persecution?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member wants Canadians to believe we are interested in sending people to be persecuted he has it completely wrong.
This government was the first to introduce in the Immigration Act the authority to require for every failed refugee claimant a case-by-case review where the person will not be deported if there is harsh or inhumane treatment awaiting that person in the country of origin.
These provisions have been introduced in the act which that hon. member voted against.

Mr. Speaker, last year the consumer and corporate affairs committee tabled a report on credit cards in Canada. The committee recommended that the government introduce legislation which would require standardized information disclosure by credit card companies.
Will the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs review the committee's recommendation and work with his provincial counterparts to introduce this badly needed consumer legislation? Consumers then would be able to compare apples with apples.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Vincent (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for his question and for his continued interest in this matter.
We are considering the committee's recommendations and I can assure the hon. member we have already started discussing potential improvements with the provinces.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
March 9, 1993

Oral Questions
The minister will know that today the treasury bill rate has reduced by 23 bases points to 5.66 per cent. This is the lowest rate for a long time.
Hear, hear.

Has the minister had any negotiations or conversations with the banks, bearing in mind that the prime rate is the rate on which business loans are judged, to see if he can get the bank rate or the prime rate down to 6 per cent and fuel our economy even faster than it presently is going?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for that question.
The rate today at 5.66 per cent is the same as it was on July 9, 1992. In so far as the prime rate is concerned, the hon. member will know that it is 6.25 per cent. It is 6 per cent in the United States. That is very narrow.
I think the hon. member knows that the banks have been leading and bringing down interest rates. The hon. member will be very encouraged to know that the spreads on short-term money are narrowing very dramatically. It is just over 2 per cent and that is a good sign as well.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance as well.
The government, without any consultation, has decided to slice $15 million from grants in lieu of taxes that the municipalities were to receive from the federal government.
Yesterday in committee finance officials admitted that they intend to do this in a completely high-handed fashion without any legislation coming before the House of Commons.
Why does the minister think that he can get away with attacking Canadian towns and cities that are going to be very badly hit by this move without even seeking parliamentary okay through legislation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are not attacking towns, villages and municipalities.
The fact is that where grants and contributions across the board have been cut by 10 per cent, in the case of the grants in lieu of taxes, we have frozen the grant at the $424 million level, the same as it was in 1992-93.
For the information of the hon. member, in 1988 that figure was $250 million. Since 1988 grants in lieu of taxes have doubled. In the last three years they have gone up by 30 per cent. All of us must tighten our belts, including the municipalities, the provinces and the federal government. As the hon. member knows, there is only one taxpayer.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Public Works and is along the same lines but not with respect to legislation.
I would like to ask about municipalities where the federal tax base is very significant, such as Oromocto in my riding, where CFB Gagetown is such a large part of the property tax base. What avenues for consultation and negotiation with his department are going to be made available to municipalities such as Oromocto to address these critical factors in their 1993-94 municipal budgets?

speakeroldname: Hon. Elmer M. MacKay (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question from my hon. colleague. He has been very concerned about his municipality, as have other members in the Chamber.
The Minister of Finance has indicated the necessity for re-evaluating the process for municipal grants in lieu of taxes because of the rapid escalation.
I have already had the opportunity to meet with the Federation of Canadian Municipalities on one occasion. I hope to meet with them again this week. We will be exploring ways to try to implement the freeze to which the Minister of Finance has referred in a fair way.
I would suggest to my colleague the best way that his municipality can try to meld itself into this approach is to work with the Federation of Canadian Municipalities as we try to come to some agreement.

I draw the attention of hon. members to the presence in the gallery of Vyacheslav Chomovil, member of the Supreme Rada of Ukraine and chairman of the Rukh Party.

March 9, 1993
Privilege
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a matter of personal privilege regarding comments made by the Minister of Supply and Services during Question Period.
It is my contention that the Minister of Supply and Services has sought to deliberately mislead members of the House and through the House, mislead members of the public with comments he has made suggesting, as he did during the Question Period to much agitation on this side of the House, notably from the member speaking, that I had passed up an opportunity to be briefed by DND on the subject of the EH-101 helicopter.
The minister began his comments by suggesting that I had missed entirely a briefing that was offered to me and to other members. Subsequently, and Hansard will show this, he altered those comments, as the agitation on this side of the House became extremely apparent, to suggest that I came late to the meeting. On the day in question, February 9, at 3.30 p.m., one-half hour after the end of Question Period, three members of Parliament from this side of the House took part in the briefing, the member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception, the member for Labrador, and myself, and three or four, I do not know the exact number, Liberal assistants.
It is true that I came into the briefing session, as the minister describes it, near the end of a slide show by DND officials. However I was there for all the questions, comments and discussion that took place between officials, parliamentarians and assistants. As well, I might point out that questions and answers were still ongoing. Notably, I was still putting questions and getting answers when the special assistant to the Minister of National Defence stood up and cut off the meeting.
With that knowledge, if the minister's comments that have been made in this House are deliberately misleading and deliberately assign motives to a member of this place, cast aspersions on a member of this place. If the
minister is not aware of all the facts then I would seek that the minister would withdraw those comments.
It is my belief, generally speaking, that members should seek and should expect the protection of the Chair when such comments are made.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Dick (Minister of Supply and Services):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I assure you I will not take any longer than the hon. member. On the week leading up to Friday, February 5 both the Liberal and New Democratic Parties were offered briefings on the EH-101. On Friday, February 5 the Liberal Party did not show for the briefing between one and two o'clock or between three and four o'clock, but the New Democratic Party, represented by the hon. member for Victoria, showed up for its briefing between two o'clock and three o'clock.
A second scheduled meeting was put forward. It was attended by the briefing team of Colonel Ross; Colonel Daly; Ray Sturgeon, ADM materiel from national defence; Harvey Nielson, PMO-DND; Gary Sager, PMO-DSS; and Commodore Garnett. This was set up for 3.30 p.m. to 4.30 p.m. on Tbesday, February 9.
At 3.30 p.m. the hon. member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception and the hon. member for Labrador entered the room and were there for the briefing until 4.25 p.m., for 55 minutes. At 4.25 p.m. the hon. member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte, who has presented this point of privilege, entered the room, 55 minutes later, at the conclusion of the slide show and the briefing. As I indicated in Question Period he was there for the questions and he did ask some questions but he missed the briefing.
Just a moment. We are in the midst of a question of privilege. Does the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond have a point of order that might assist me?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that the Chair heard point of order. I wish to add some facts with regard to the point of privilege raised by my colleague, in view of the fact that I am intricately involved in some of the facts which the minister has alluded to.
I am wondering if the Chair under the guise of fairness would give me an opportunity to present my intervention.
March 9, 1993
Somebody said point of order and that is what I did hear. If the hon. member is speaking on this particular point of privilege I will most certainly hear him.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Supply and Services is correct in certain facts on this issue.
I know the Minister of Supply and Services to be an honourable minister and he will recall that on February 2 his colleague, the Minister of National Defence, was the lead minister who offered a briefing to members of Parliament on both sides of the House. On February 3 I instructed a member of my staff to make contact with the minister's office in the person of Mr. Kevin Phillips, who is the associate director of the Directorate of Parliamentary Affairs, to set up the briefing.
On February 5, as the House leader for the Official Opposition I sent a letter to the gentleman in question. I sent not only a letter but a fax as well.
On February 9, which the minister has referred to, at 3.30 in the afternoon, not only was my colleague who has raised the point of privilege present but my colleagues, the member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception and the member for Labrador, were also present along with other Liberal assistants.
The hon. minister opposite shakes his head and says no. Was the minister there? No, the minister was not there. I want to make it perfectly clear so that the Minister of Supply and Services, who during Question Period made reference to my colleague and who I know is an honourable person, will stand in his place and admit that he referred to the hon. member in question as lying. That is the word he used, in fact he used it on two specific occasions.
In conclusion, with regard to the point my colleague has raised, the meeting which the minister has referred to has cast aspersions upon my colleague from Newfoundland. His activities as an active member of this House of Commons were cut short, not by members of the opposition but by the legislative assistant to the Minister of National Defence. I would hope, on the basis of fairness and of the title "honourable", that the minister opposite would stand in his place and apologize to this member and to members of this House.
Privilege

Mr. Speaker, it is most appropriate that the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond would come to the defence of the hon. member for Humber- St. Barbe-Baie Verte. I can understand.
There is an error in one of his facts. He said that the hon. member was there at 3.30 p.m. Be that as it may, I have offered before in Question Period and I offer again, if they want to bring this up in the standing committee and go into all the details I would be more than delighted to do that and we can have all the officials there. If by some chance I overstated a case and made a reference which is unparliamentary because of the errors which all so often happen in stating of fact in this case by the members in question then I would certainly want to apologize to the House. I would not want to be unparliamentary. But they should get their facts right.

I wonder if the hon. minister could assist me a little bit and explain exactly whether the minister is withdrawing anything that he has said. I understand there is an apology for any error he may have made. I think I divined an apology if he did say what he has been accused of saying, but I want it absolutely clear on the record.
Absolutely, Mr. Speaker. I agree. If I said anything that was unparliamentary I withdraw it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as a spokesperson for the Official Opposition I wish to thank the hon. member opposite, who has made an unequivocal apology to my colleague in this House for his unparliamentary language.
Perhaps on behalf of all hon. members I can thank the minister and the hon. members for Cape Breton-East Richmond and Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles A. Langlois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. In Oral Question Period, the member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte asked the Minister of National Defence a question and he said this:

"Mr. Minister, you haven't told Canadians the full truth".

Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, I understand that accusing someone of not telling the truth is considered unparliamentary. I therefore ask the member for Humber-St. Barbe- Baie Verte to withdraw what he said, if I heard it correctly, and apologize appropriately to the minister.

In response to the hon. member's intervention, without presuming too far on the general customs here, the hon. member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte is not in the House at the moment. Perhaps we could come back to this matter at another appropriate moment.

Mr. Speaker, I want to raise with you for your guidance comments that were made yesterday in committee with respect to testimony dealing with Bill C-113.
During testimony by officials from the Department of Finance with respect to that bill, which has the effect of freezing a number of different expenditures, I raised a question regarding the freeze to grants in lieu of taxation to municipalities and how that will be brought before the House of Commons for debate or discussion.
I was answered at that stage with the following comment: "There is no legislation either in the House or contemplated".

Mr. Speaker, I have a few words concerning this piece of legislation at its final third reading and passage through the House.
The bill itself really will do nothing for Canada Post or mail service in Canada. It will do absolutely nothing. Who invented the legislation or who came up with the idea is unknown to members of the House. The substance of the legislation is to offer something to employees, who are not defined under the legislation, amounting to 10 per cent of the shares of the Canada Post Corporation.
The Government of Canada would of course retain 90 per cent of the shares of the corporation.
The reason we do not agree with this legislation is that we believe it is a waste of time for the Government of Canada and the House of Commons of Canada to be discussing this non-issue in this Chamber and be taking up the time and money of the people of Canada to perform a duty such as this when not even the unions representing the employees are in agreement with it. It does nothing for postal service in Canada. It does not improve the record of Canada Post, which is a very bad record as far as mail delivery is concerned, as far as lost

mail is concerned and as far as the destruction of Canada Post and the post office in Canada is concerned.
We have gone from a corporation that had as its main objective the delivery of mail in Canada to a corporation that is now closing down post offices and that has reduced mail service in Canada. We have seen the introduction of so-called supermailboxes in a lot of the rural areas in Canada. We have seen the closing of our post offices that meant so much to people in our rural and urban areas of this country.
Perhaps the most important reason why we are opposed to this legislation is that it will really not do what it appears to be doing. I say that because the shares being offered to the employees-it is not defined and perhaps is meant to be management-will not be voting shares. The say in the corporation will not mean anything at all as far as the administration is concerned, as far as the day-to-day operations of the corporation are concerned or as far as anything is concerned. It will do nothing to lift the veil of secrecy surrounding the corporation.
What is the salary of the chief executive officer of Canada Post, for example? Nobody knows except the chief executive officer of Canada Post. Nobody else knows. Who else might know? The cabinet might know. A committee of the cabinet might know what his salary is. I would say it is somewhere in the order of about $380,000 per year. It is probably about that. The salaries of the chief executive officer, the chief operating officer and the people at the top in Canada Post, paid for from the taxpayers' pockets, have been substantially increased over the years. There has been a substantial increase from about 1987.
The salary jumped. As I recall, the CEO's salary was somewhere in the order of $180,000 per year in 1987-1 could be wrong-give or take $50,000. As I mentioned, nobody knows what his salary is. It jumped by about $100,000 a year in about a year and a half and then it jumped again because the margins increased by that amount.
The people talked about in this legislation are the employees who are being given a share in the corporation. The employees of Canada Post are now being told

Mr. Speaker, earlier today I was asked to speak for 10 minutes on this particular bill, but the events of the day have taken me to speak double that time. Actually I am quite happy to have my time extended. It prompted me to call around the community and find out just exactly what the status was. It is not that I did not know before, but some gruesome details were brought forward today and I welcome the opportunity to raise them.
All members want to highlight their own constituencies and talk about the problems they may have in a particular area. One that has certainly bedevilled me in the four years and four months I have served in this position is Canada Post, the post office workers and the customers. I can safely say after finding out today what is going on that we have reached the zenith of dissatisfaction with Canada Post.
Before you rule me out of order, Mr. Speaker, I want to address Bill C-73 specifically. It suggests the employees will be able to voluntarily buy up to 10 per cent of the shares of Canada Post. Most of the employees in Canada Post are eager to get a buy-out, not a buy-in. The morale is that bad. The harassment of workers is that bad.
It is difficult for us to appreciate the fact that many of us enjoy some freedom in our jobs. Some of us enjoy a great deal of freedom; others have very little freedom. I do not know if I could handle an occupation that measures the number of steps I take in a day. If I take 10 steps too many or 10 steps too few my route might be changed and that has an impact on all of the mail carriers. What kind of flexibility does an employee have working for Canada Post?
I suspect that veiy few will be buying into the company. You do not buy into a company that obviously is looking to sell out to other people. Bill C-73 no doubt is addressing the beginning of privatization of Canada Post. It has been quoted to me: "There is no doubt we want to sell it but we have to make it very profitable first". That is the bottom line. If it is profitable then it can be sold, but at this point in time it is creating a great deal of problems. In the name of efficiency, in the name of better service, it is going in the opposite direction. What I have uncovered today certainly proves to me and to the residents of my community that it is absolutely true.

Once in a while we have the business community on one side, the residents on another and the unions on yet another side perhaps. In this one everyone agrees that the system has deteriorated. The saga of Canada Post is a sad one.
I remember four years ago. I was new on the job. I fell for it. Canada Post approached me and said it wanted to build a new post office for Sault Ste. Marie. I thought that was great. I talked it over and we found it was reasonably good. It was going to invest $5 million on the outskirts of the community. It would impact on some workers but over-all it looked like an investment in the community.
I foolishly went forward and made the announcement in front of the old post office, a landmark in our community. I said that Canada Post had chosen to invest $5 million in our community. It would improve efficiency. Everything would be better for all of us and it would still maintain the great heritage structure.
I made that announcement for Canada Post, like a fool, like a gullible dolt. I did it. Two months later, much to my embarrassment-it did not seem to bother Canada Post-it said it was sorry but it had changed its mind.
That is good corporate planning. It was going to invest $5 million but two months later the plan was changed. I then asked what the plan would be. A new facility would not be built; the old facility would be renovated. I thought that did not sound bad and asked what exactly would be done.
We went to the site. I was advised that $0.75 million or whatever would be invested to improve the docking bays. Once again I was hesitant but asked if the office downtown would be maintained. Great, it would still be there. It would still be the focal point of our community, as the post office is in so many communities across this country. I was told that things were not going to change. It would be business as usual but we would have a better facility.
This time at least I did not make the announcement. I did not fall for it. Canada Post made the announcement. There was a certain amount of apprehension on behalf of the workers but it looked good.

The saga continues. The building is renovated and rehabilitated. However, what is happening is that Canada Post in its corporate decision making felt it had to centralize the mail. It had to be shipped off a couple of hundred miles to Sudbury. It had to centralize in the name of efficiency, but if efficiency were improved some Canada Post employees would have to be laid off.

Marie to Sudbury to Sault Ste. Marie. The bottom line is if a letter has to go one mile away within the community it may have to go 900 miles to get there". Now is that efficient? The minister said on May 1, 1992: "It is a proven vehicle for improving morale if we allow people to buy shares in the company". They said Canada Post was now going to become a corporate citizen. It was going to sponsor events in our community. That would make everybody happy and everybody would love Canada Post. It sounded good and I asked what else was going to happen.
They said there was a new commercial outlet system, but our post office would have to be downgraded. If we wanted to buy stamps at the main post office we would have to buy $300 worth. We were told that outlets would be put all over the place and that this would be better for us and for business. Canada Post would have sales people go out. It was going to commercialize and privatize it. They would go out and sell stamps to all the businesses.
That did not sound all that great to me. Well, certainly it did not. Within one month that commercial enterprise is now dead. I did not find out until today that it is dead. The proponents told me just a month ago that this would be a raving success. We have not heard from the proponents, the workers told me. It was the workers who asked whether I knew that this was now gone.
I was not fooled this time. I was not fooled, but once again Canada Post has struck a death-knell in the community as far as postal services are concerned. I

Even after they have filed letters from psychiatrists saying that part of the problem is that they are under mental health stress and are having psychiatric problems but they are being phoned repeatedly and threatened that the documentation with respect to their illness is not proper and that their jobs are in jeopardy.

In view of these facts there has been, at least in the postal services I am aware of, a deterioration in the morale of employees. Of course along with a deterioration in morale there is an increasing lack of communication between management and the employees. With the
breakdown in communication there is increasing animosity.
The member has obviously had considerable experience with the post office in his area. Does he feel that the share concept is actually going to assist in improving the morale of the postal workers, or does he think better management practices would be more to the point?

Mr. Speaker, once in a while I am sure we are accused of exaggerating to make a point. However on this particular issue there is no exaggeration. What the member for Surrey North has said is absolutely true. I have shared those experiences. I think other members in the House right now would say the same has happened to them.
The morale is negligible. It is not a pretty picture. We have created villains of a group that is not guilty of anything. Many people regard them as malcontents and say they act inappropriately, do the wrong things and should be thankful for having wonderful jobs. The working environment at Canada Post is horrendous. There is no trust.
The hon. member talked about arbitrary reassessment. That is what it is, totally arbitrary. When people are ill they cannot have normal sick days; there is harassment. What is the goal in that? I am not sure. One has to wonder. What is the goal? Is it to make them sufficiently unhappy in the work environment that it is easier to reduce the number of staff?
I had a individual come into my office and say that he wanted out. I said: "You are only 45 years old", and he said: "I do not care. Whatever they offer me I am getting out because my mental health will not survive what they are putting me through".
These are true stories. Everything that is said is the absolute truth.
They will not get UI.

They very likely will not get any UI because of leaving their positions. I hope that is straightened out. It is a matter of trust. There is absolutely no trust between the employer and the employee. I have learned as well to completely mistrust Canada Post Corporation and its spokespeople.
March 9, 1993

Mr. Speaker, listening to this debate today has been an education for me. The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie and other members have spoken in the House today about Canada Post and the experiences they have had in their particular ridings. I have certainly had similar experiences.
For a government and for a corporation that are trying to endear themselves to the Canadian public they are certainly not doing a very good job. The stories recounted by the member for Sault Ste. Marie are reminiscent of stories taking place in my own riding.
It is true that there is no trust between the employer and the employee. There is no trust between Canada Post and the public. There is no trust between the government and the public. Much of this has to be blamed directly on the government and, through its directions, directly on Canada Post.
The bill before us now contains the idea of sharing the wealth with Canada Post employees. It is nothing more than a smoke-screen for the proposal to privatize Canada Post. It is part of the slippery slope of privatization. For those people who do not believe Canada Post is to be privatized I simply want to cite a couple of quotes.
On May 1, 1992 an article in The Ottawa Citizen contained the following quote of the minister responsible for Canada Post: "Harvie Andre insisted that immediate privatization is not in the cards". He went on to state: "If I had to bet I would bet that in the next couple of decades you will see post offices being privatized all over the world. I would not mind seeing Canada first".
That is quite a statement. When the government makes that kind of statement we can rest assured that privatization is just down the road. After all, let us remember the words of the Prime Minister in 1985 when he stated: "Some people want to buy the CBC. The CBC is not for sale. Air Canada is not for sale". Air Canada was for sale. It has been sold. It is now a private company.
The bill today is simply one more step along the way toward privatization. It is a thinly veiled sham that the government is trying to put before us to hide privatization. In fact the minister responsible is really not hiding it at all. I remember the minister commenting a year or so ago that until we could get rid of more rural post
Government Orders
offices, until we could get rid of more corporate post offices and until we could raise the profits of Canada Post there would be no privatization. Those were amazing statements.
The bill in front of us is supposed to help with employee relations. What will it do? It will allow the employees of Canada Post to buy 10 per cent of the shares of the corporation. Employees are not defined. We do not know exactly who the employees are. We do not know whether it is simply management or whether it is everyone right down to the person just hired yesterday. As well there is no indication of what kind of shares the employees will have once they get them. We do know they will not be voting shares.
If a government is supposed to have confidence in its employees and is to sell them 10 per cent of the shares then we would think they would be given voting rights with those shares. It is only 10 per cent, but no, they will be non-voting shares. Will they get dividends from these shares? There is no indication as to whether they will or not.
The fact is that Canada Post has made a profit for three of the last four years. If one is a shareholder in the corporation, then one expects to get some dividends, but no, there is no indication of that. Chances are, if I was to make a guess, there will be no dividends from those shares.
Canada Post and the government did not even consult with the union as to the sale of these shares. There was no discussion or consultation. There was just an arbitrary decision to sell these shares.
If Canada Post and the government wanted to see relations improved with these employees then something should be done about the grievances that exist in Canada Post. I was amazed, as were members in my caucus, to discover the number of grievances that exist in Canada Post. People in Canada might think maybe there would be 1,000 or 2,000 grievances. No, there are more than that. There are more than 10,000 grievances. Are there
20,000	or 40,000? No. There are only 50,000 employees in the whole corporation, but there are more than that many grievances. Double it. There are 100,000 grievances outstanding against Canada Post. That is almost two grievances for every employee who works for Cana-

Government Orders
da Post. It is unbelievable. Those grievances are backed up for years.
If Canada Post wants to improve relations with employees, then why does it not start to look at some of the grievances and start removing some of the reasons for those grievances in the first place? There cannot be
100.000	grievances that have no merit. I doubt it very much. I am sure there are some grievances that do not have as much merit as others, but there cannot be
100.000	grievances against Canada Post that have no merit.
This idea of improving employee relations is simply nonsense. It simply makes it that much easier for the government to privatize Canada Post when the time arrives.
In talking about relations with the public, I think it was last year when Canada Post had a strike. Canada Post employees offered that during the strike they would still deliver unemployment insurance cheques, Canada pension cheques and so on, but no, the government would not allow that. What it did was to spend millions of dollars to set up these depots. We had the case of seniors and disabled people being forced to stand for up to two hours in sweltering heat waiting to receive a cheque at a depot. In many instances when they got to the front of the line they were told: "Sorry, the cheque is not here so come back tomorrow". That does not endear Canada Post to the public.
My riding of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, like other ridings across the country, is largely rural. We have had a number of rural post office closings. In fact, in the last five years across this country, 25 per cent of all the post offices that existed prior to that time have now been closed. That is one in four.
Many times these post offices were closed not because there was a need to close the post office or because the post office was not being used, but simply because the post office had been provided with what they call a natural opportunity. This means that either the postmaster or postmistress had died or retired or something of that nature.
When these events occur, Canada Post will roll into town and have a public meeting. It will tell the people at the meeting that it is here to improve their service. I have been to a number of them in my own riding. It is going to improve the service. When the people in the
community say that they are happy with their service, then Canada Post simply says: "No, we have to close the post office, but we are going to improve your service".
What happens is that they tell them that they are going to consult with them. There is no real consultation. The only consultation is that they have the opportunity of setting up a retail postal outlet which means a post office being placed in a store somewhere or they are going to have mailboxes and that is their choice.
In my riding the communities have naively thought that they could deal with Canada Post and work with it. I know of one situation in my riding where the people in the community said: "Look, we will give you a free building. We will buy the building and give it to Canada Post. Canada Post can keep the building as long as it operates a corporate post office out of it". There was no deal.
We had another situation where people in another community said: "Look, we will give you one of the staff people from our town hall who can work with Canada Post when it is busy". There was no deal.
We have had situations where people in the communities have said: "Look, we will take less service. Cut the hours down and cut the number of days down". There was no deal.
Yet Canada Post will tell these communities that the reason it is closing its post offices is because it is not making money. It will not tell you how much that community brings in. It will not tell you how much the post office in that community costs, but it will say that it has to close it.
I know that Canada Post wants to make a profit. Let us say it said: "Look, we have to make a profit and we would like to keep this post office open and we would like to provide the best service we can so here is what the bottom line is in this community. It brings in x thousands of dollars and it costs x thousands of dollars". One would find a lot of communities willing to work with Canada Post.
We know we are in debt in this country. We know we have an annual deficit that has not dropped in the last nine years or perhaps it marginally dropped in the last nine years. The people in the community will say: "Let's
March 9, 1993

work with Canada Post to help Canada Post provide a service". That is fair but Canada Post will not give any details.
This idea of saying that it wants to provide a better service is a myth. In fact it is a lie. It is not true. The fact is that Canada Post wants to privatize as many corporate post offices as it can in this country and in doing so make it easier to eventually sell that corporation.
I want to talk a bit about the city of Moose Jaw. In the city of Moose Jaw-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I apologize for interrupting the hon. member. I just wanted to formally designate tomorrow as an allotted day or supply day.

I thought the minister was going to rise and tell me that things would not change in Moose Jaw and that the post office would remain. I am disappointed.
I wanted to comment about the city of Moose Jaw. In the city of Moose Jaw we have our corporate post office. It is viable and it is running. However we have been advised, not by the officials at Canada Post but by other people who have found out information and let us know, that the post office in Moose Jaw is going to close and the wicket service will be gone. We have not heard that announcement yet. If one calls the public relations people at Canada Post they will deny it. They will say that there has been no decision made yet. However, that is nonsense because the decision has been made.
The fact is that not only is Canada Post going to close the corporate post office but it is going to close all the sub-post offices that exist in Moose Jaw. One of them has existed in Moose Jaw since 1928 and it is going to be closed. Where is it going to go? It is going to set up four retail postal outlets in the city of Moose Jaw. This has not been announced publicly yet but that is what the plan is. Where are they going to go? They are going to go to places like Shoppers Drug Mart and Bi-Rite Drugs. I have nothing against Shoppers Drug Mart and Bi-Rite Drugs except that I find it strange that these retail postal outlets find their way into these national chains.

National or international?

In many cases they are international chains. The fact is that some of these sub-post offices have long been in business. One in particular has been there since 1928. It is in Carr's Confectionery in Moose Jaw. Mr. Carr opened a confectionery business in the early twenties and worked hard at that business. His son has taken it over and his son is now running that confectionery.
These are people who live in the community, who contribute to the community and whose children go to school in the community. These people put a lot of hours into their work and they put that money back into the community. It is a small business, a good small business, and it provides a good service.
It is denying those small businesses a chance for a post office. It is already a sub-post office but it is going to franchise them all. It is going to deny those small businesses a chance for the franchise and give it to a national or international chain.
This is a government that is supposed to be for small business. This certainly does not bode well for small business. If a government wants to assist small business then this is not the way it should go about doing it.
I find it ironic. I must say I find it insulting that when one phones up Regina and talks to the Canada Post folks they say there have been no decisions made yet. No decisions have been made yet, but the ripples are there. I have talked to people who own the sub-post offices. I have talked to some of the union people. I have even talked to people in Canada Post who will talk to me and who have told me privately that this is what is happening.
If Canada Post really wants to improve its relationship with the employees of the corporation and with the people of this country then it had better take a new attitude.
First of all, it should be honest with Canadians. If it is going to privatize the corporation then it should come out and say that the objective is to privatize this corporation and this is the plan for privatization. Let the people know what is going on. Do not give these stories that are totally unbelievable.

March 9, 1993
Government Orders
In fact when Canada Post is confronted with the facts, it still denies it. Oh no, there is no decision made yet. Be honest with the people.
The other thing is to not be so arrogant. I have been told by people who in trying to save their post office talked to Canada Post and were told: "You can always complain to your MP but it will not do any good because we are going to do what we want anyway". Thanks a bunch.
That is an arrogant attitude that I find personally insulting and I know the people in those rural communities find it insulting. If Canada Post wants to improve relationships with the country, it is going about it in exactly the wrong way. Until it improves relationships with its employees and until it improves relationships with the people of this country, it is going to find itself being kicked in the shins like it has been today.
In closing I want to say that Canada Post was here to provide a service to the people of Canada. That was its original intent. It was to provide good mail service. That is not its objective today. Its objective is purely and simply to make a profit. It may step on people in the process. They may be Canadians who receive mail, whether they are in small businesses and have run sub-post offices for some time or for a short time, or they may be employees in its way. That is irrelevant. It may also be an MP who tries to deal with it. However Canada Post is going to "do what it wants", to quote its words.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask my colleague a very simple, straightforward question. Why has Canada Post lost the trust of the consumers and the employees to such a great extent in Canada?
We do not find that any part of the community or any of its employees think of it as a service that contributes to Canada. I wonder if my colleague can tell me why he thinks it has lost its trust to such an extent all across Canada and not only here.

Mr. Speaker, the loss of trust that Canadians have in Canada Post did not happen overnight. It took a lot of effort and it took a lot of doing by Canada Post. It was done in a number of areas.
With respect to the employees, that lack of trust has come about as a result of the inability or the unwillingness of both the government and Canada Post to deal honestly and openly with the employees. If there are
100,000	grievances in a corporation that is an awful lot, particularly when there are only 50,000 employees. The employees have lost trust because of Canada Post's refusal to deal openly with the union.
There was no consultation with the union on this bill at all, no consultation on how services could be improved for the employees or how to better improve the lot of the employee. There was no discussion at all.
With respect to rural Canadians, it has done a very good job of losing trust. It could not have done a better job if it had tried to lose trust with rural Canadians, because it has closed 25 per cent of all rural post offices in this country in the last five years without consultation with rural Canadians.
In fact it is the opposite. It comes into a community and tries to tell it how its service will be improved. People actually laugh at these meetings because Canada Post comes in and says it is going to improve service by closing the post office. People simply scratch their heads. Sometimes in these communities there will be 150 to 200 people at a meeting wondering what is happening to their post office.
They came to the meeting having received a letter from Canada Post in the mail inviting them to a meeting on this particular night to discuss the future of Canada Post. But they are not being consulted, they are being told. They are being hoodwinked. They leave the meeting feeling bitter and confused. That has done an awful lot to hurt the reputation of Canada Post with rural Canadians.
The other way is through public relations. There are people at Canada Post in management with whom I have dealt who are very good. I do not want to label all of them. However, there are others who really should not be in PR. I do not know where it hires some of these people but it should not even interview them as far as public relations is concerned. They are arrogant and they are not helpful. They simply tell people who want to save their post office to go ahead and call their MP. It will not do any good because it is going to do what it wants anyway.
March 9, 1993

That has also hurt its reputation. Canada Post now has such a poor reputation in Canada that it is going to take a long time to build it up. It is obvious that neither Canada Post nor this government really have any concern about Canada Post's public relations with Canadians. If they did they would not act the way they do. This bill would not have been brought in, and certainly not without consultation with the employees.

Mr. Speaker, I am wondering if the previous speaker has any information as to whether Canada Post has any standards when it contracts with a private operator in a retail outlet.
It was mentioned that there have been difficulties. There was a situation in my riding of Surrey North in which one in a large chain of drugstores had a postal outlet which had been there for a number of years. Then a new owner came in. The drugstore changed hands. Nine women were working there, some of them had been working there for 10 years.
Immediately the new owner arbitrarily started to reduce their wages, reduce the number of hours and change the seniority pattern in terms of working of shifts and was then surprised when the women got hold of one of the more progressive unions and started a unionization drive. They were on strike for nearly 18 months.
That big drugstore chain made a decision that it would shut that whole drugstore down rather than ever agree to allow a first contract with those employees. These were basically postal workers.
Does the member know whether the postal corporation when it is putting in postal outlets in retail stores has any standards about working conditions, wages and the normal things that an employee would expect?

Mr. Speaker, I do not believe Canada Post has any real standards at all. Not only is that true with employees but there is a scenario being played out in Moose Jaw right now that really astounds me and makes me wonder whether Canada Post has any idea of what it is doing.
There is a business called Ottawa Real Estate which has been in Moose Jaw since 1909. This business is a well-established business and has been in the same family for years. The present proprietor, Glen McRitch-
Government Orders
ie, is a very outstanding and well-respected businessman in the community. He has a sub-post office in his store but he has been advised that the sub-post office is going to close and he will not get the franchise.
That post office is the only post office on Main Street. East of Main Street there are a number of senior high-rises. He put out a petition and in just a few days had over 1,200 signatures of people who said they would like to use the post office. When he called up Canada Post it said that his post office was not wheelchair accessible. He said it was, that there was a four-foot door and a ramp which people ride up in their motorized chairs to get service.
Canada Post then said that he could only give 300 square feet. He said he would give them 1,000 square feet. It replied that his hours were not acceptable. He then said he would open his business for postal business any hours that Canada Post asked him to. It accused him of not putting up a sign. He said he never said that he would not put up a sign. He would put up a sign. Furthermore, he said that the post office in Moose Jaw is the only bilingual post office in the city and that people from CFB Moose Jaw-and there are a number of francophones who live in CFB Moose Jaw-come to use his post office. Canada Post said it is going to close it. That is unbelievable.
Since Glen McRitchie took over the post office the business has improved and profits have gone up for Canada Post in that area, and yet it is being closed. This is a situation in which the business has been in Moose Jaw since 1909, it is wheelchair accessible, it is bilingual, it could provide more space if Canada Post wanted it, it would put up a sign and stay open any hours Canada Post wants it to and yet Canada Post wants to close it. In addition, it is the only post office on Main Street.
If Canada Post has standards I do not know where they are. They must have been lost or have disappeared because nobody seems to be following them.

Mr. Speaker, as my colleague has just been saying, this debate on Bill C-73 is a debate about the service provided to Canadian citizens by Canada Post.
Over the years Canada Post has been one of the proud institutions of Canada and has provided the kind of service that everybody thought could not be duplicated anywhere around the world and was not duplicated anywhere around the world. The people who worked for Canada Post were a proud part of that organization. They know that the kind of service they used to provide is still possible. However they also know that there is not much chance that the present Canada Post is going to provide that kind of service.
They also know that the employees of Canada Post no longer have any trust, nor do the consumers have any trust, in the ability of Canada Post to provide the kind of service they have learned to expect. They now no longer expect it.
This bill is the first step toward complete privatization. Privatization has been going on for quite some time. The privatization has been of the outlets until now, and a certain number of the post office buildings and so on in many towns and cities.
The city of Prince Albert has a population of something over 30,000 people. It does not have an official corporate post office. It has a series of franchises that are supposed to provide the same kind of service but only marginally do so in many cases.
This bill is the first step toward complete privatization. We know it is privatization because we have models before us. The steps started early. They started a long time ago with the Liberal government of Pierre Trudeau which transformed the corporation from an agency of the government to a Crown corporation.
Now we are going the next step. We are going to sell shares in this Crown corporation. Granted, at the beginning these shares are going to be available only to people who are employees of the Crown corporation.
If we cut down the population of the employees by two-thirds in the last five years there are not too many of them who trust they will have a job within the next while, so why should they consider buying shares?
Then there is the next step after selling or providing shares. If members read the bill they will find that there are two steps in this. There is the decision to make the shares available. This means that the government has to take the assets of that company and divide them into so many parts, with each one represented by a share.
Then it sends 10 per cent of those shares to the employees and the other 90 per cent is for the government to keep. How long does it keep them? There is the question. How long will it keep them? Next year the government might say: "Aha, now that we have made this corporation appealing to the private sector and since we have downgraded the service to the extent that Canada Post does not have to provide this kind of service any longer, we can provide service to parts of Canada that will be adequate and make some money on it".
Canada is a big country. There are thousands and thousands of miles between communities in some cases. There are many small communities between the large communities and many small communities before those.
What we believe we can have in Canada and what we understand that we can have is the same kind of service in every one of those communities. We believe that Canada Post should be able to take the mail to every community. We recognize that we will only get it once a week in some places. Those who have lived in northern Canada will realize that sometimes they get it only once a month. Canada Post was delivering to their community but that is no longer true. Canada Post is not the same as it was before.
As I said, this is a step toward privatization. The model that we can point directly to is Air Canada, and that has been well documented here this morning and this afternoon. With Air Canada, the first step was the division into shares that could be sold to the employees. We were told that Air Canada was not for sale. We know what happened there.
Canada Post has many problems besides the selling of its shares. This bill does nothing and in fact it is intended to do nothing about any of the problems which Canada Post has. The self-proclaimed pit bull terrier that a member was talking about a little earlier said that this
March 9, 1993

will improve employee-employer relations. Since Canada Post is offering shares, it suggested that since the employees own part of the corporation maybe they will work a little harder and the service will be a little better.
Over the last 10 years Canada Post has undermined the trust of those employees to such an extent that offering them 10 per cent of the shares, which are valueless unless they can get a dividend-and it seems unlikely that they will get a dividend-does not sweeten the pot in the least bit. Consequently there is unlikely to be any improved labour relations. The very fact it did not ask the employees whether they wanted this to happen is a good indication it did not even intend to improve labour relations.
The employees ask why would they buy the shares if with the shares there is not some kind of job security. If this bill goes through and the shares are available to employees it does not mean that if they have a good chunk of shares they are guaranteed a job. The next day or the next week you may be laid off. No security goes with these shares.
I started my speech by saying that the debate was about service. It is obvious that this bill is not about service and that is why any self-respecting member in this House would oppose it. The post office is something that every one of us has in our community. It has been downgraded to the extent that none of us can be proud of the fact that we represent a government that has a corporation that gives this kind of service to a community.
It is ironic that this bill is suggesting that the company give its employees an opportunity to buy into this company. First of all it is losing money and is laying people off as quickly as it possibly can. Every privatization of an outlet reduces the number of employees that Canada Post has.
This process of privatization of outlets, if you talk to Canada Post, is done by consultation. Like my colleague from Moose Jaw, I have been there. This government has given the term consultation a bad name. It asks the community to come forward and then decides what should be done about this particular post office. The citizens of those communities have been duped before. They know they are going to be duped again, but they go to the meetings. They have a certain amount of trust in government. They go. They have municipal governments
Government Orders
and they have provincial governments and they have a federal government that they can depend on to give them service. The government will tell them they have two or three alternatives.
I am talking now about a meeting that I went to not too many months ago in the small town of Tway. I attended other meetings in the small town of Hoey and one in Cudworth. They are small towns in my constituency. In each of those cases citizens were told they had three alternatives. The first was that, they could have a business outlet where they could have a franchise post office. It does not pay very much for that and in many of those cases not one of those stores or one of those businesses really wanted the post office. They would take the post office because it had some value, because people have to come there and it is a service to the community that they as good citizens feel they should give. The second was that those green boxes beside the road. The third was the post office is closed and the citizens would go to the next community to get their mail and their service.
Before these Canada Post officials came, they had already decided that what this community was going to get was a franchise post office. They come before the community and tell a few lies about how good it is going to be after they have privatized this post office, how much better the service is going to be and then they proceed to tell the community what they had intended to do all along. They tell the community it has a choice: number one, number two or number three. The community is going to choose the least offensive of those three alternatives, which was what was intended all along. In many cases it does not reduce the cost to Canada Post.
That in itself is another complaint that I think we should air here today and should be aired as often as possible. The value of service in a post office is not valued by the number of pieces of mail that is handled. We did a two-hour check in one of the post offices in my region. It sold 100 stamps and handled 2,000 pieces of mail. That does not sound like a very good paying proposition but we were told it was better than usual. That sounds like a losing proposition except that every one of those 2,000 pieces of mail had been paid for as well. That post office was told that it was not making any

March 9, 1993
Government Orders
money because it was not selling very many stamps. It is very unfair.
At one of the meetings that I attended the Canada Post representatives said they had seen no reduction in service in any of the post office changes that they had made in my area. That is a direct lie. I am a farmer. I used to have rural delivery to my door. I no longer have rural delivery to my door. Is that not a reduction in service? When I had rural delivery to my door the service I received stamps, parcels delivered to the door and even some good companionship with the mail carrier as he came around a couple of times a week. Now I drive 20 miles to get my mail and any other postal service I need.
The little community of Brockington in my constituency had a small rural post office. Now it has outdoor green boxes. Is that not a reduction in service? People have to go to Melfort, about 18 miles away, to get service and stamps:
Down the road a little way is another small town where the service was reduced from eight hours a day to twenty hours a week. In other words, the service was cut in half. The Canada Post official stood before the community and said no community in this area had its service reduced. Is the reduction of service from 40 hours a week to 20 hours a week not a reduction in service? We are being told that there are no changes in the post offices and no reduced services.
Let us go back to the consultations I had places like Tway, Hoey and Cudworth. The communities were told they would have something to say about what they got. They did not. In the end they were told what they would get.
My colleagues from every party across the country can tell you exactly the same thing. I know that members of the Conservative Party faced exactly the same kind of treatment from the Canada Post officials in their communities as we did in ours.
This kind of manipulation by civil servants is straight arrogance. They are saying to the people in my communities that they are not smart enough to know what is good for them, they are not smart enough to know that the post office is making money. These civil servants are telling the people that the post office is not making money. They will lie to you and you will not even know
that you are being lied to. It is straight arrogance and it is treating the people of Canada in a way that they should not be treated.
It is a treatment of people in a way that we as members of Parliament abhor and should do something about. Passing this bill is not doing something about it, it is just keeping it going on and on.
A corporation's survival is dependent upon the trust that the consumers and the employees have in it. The House resumed from Thursday, December 3, 1992, consideration of the motion of Mr. Caccia:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should, for the benefit of Canadian fisheries, urgently take the necessary steps to ratify the International Law of the Sea, and urge other nations to do so in order to reach the 60 signatures required for the Law of the Sea to come into force.
Private Members' Business

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak in favour of the motion introduced by the hon. member for Davenport, an international statesman for sustainable development if I could give him that title. By introducing this motion he demonstrates that knows what he is talking about.
Canada boasts the longest coastline in the world, 151,489 miles, and the second largest undersea shelf, 2.5 million square miles. Yet we still have not ratified the Law of the Sea.
It is ironic and quite hypocritical of Canada to withhold ratification considering we signed the document in 1982 along with 119 other countries. The hon. member for Davenport tells me that as of March 1993, 56 countries will have ratified. All we need is four more countries and it would become law.
Canada worked very hard to bring many of these countries to the bargaining table in order to secure, among other things, protection of the ocean environment and sovereignty of our coastal waters.
It is also worth noting that some of Canada's best and brightest diplomats dedicated their careers to the signing of this treaty. Now, more than 11 years after the fact, Canada's best interests still lie in the ratification of the Law of the Sea.
This is a highly complex treaty, yet it affirms three fundamental principles. Many Canadians can relate to the first principle, which is the affirmation of our sovereign rights to the waters along our coastline. In the past Canada has been forced to take a number of unilateral actions to protect our rights, often when other countries infringe on our territory or threaten our environment.
For example in 1969, the American supertanker Manhattan sailed through our northwest passage without Canadian consent or notification. What if this giant oil tanker spilled her cargo all over the Canadian Arctic waters? Who would pay for the initial clean up? Who would compensate native peoples for ruining their lifestyles for generations, if maybe not for life?
Canada did respond unilaterally when the Trudeau government brought in the 1970 Arctic Waters Pollution Protection Act. This action was not welcomed by the international community, particularly by the United

March 9, 1993
Private Members' Business
States. However, in the wake of the environmental catastrophe caused by the 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill in Alaska I think the Liberal government showed considerable foresight over 20 years ago.
In addition to the rights we claimed in the 1970 Arctic waters act the Law of the Sea acknowledges the 200-mile limit Canada established to protect our fishing industry. Right now the 200-mile limit is customarily respected but the Law of the Sea would establish an exclusive economic zone, EEZ as it is known. It represents the highest long-term economic gain for Canada.
In addition to the economic gains, however, the economic zones would in effect make environmental protection a duty. It would place the responsibility on coastal states to clean up their act and treat our limited ocean resources with respect.
I would like to go on in greater detail but I must proceed to the second major principle of this treaty. That is to make some portion of the sea floor and the seabed part of the common heritage of mankind and to share these resources with all countries.
This part of the treaty recognizes the economic gap between the northern and southern hemisphere and the fact that developing countries must be given a shot at developing natural resources before more technologically advanced countries scoop up all the wealth first.
Over the last week we have had two important speakers. Today it was a doctor who has practised in developing countries and last week it was Mr. Hue, the author of the report Human Development 1992. Tliese experts are telling us to permit these countries to stand on their own feet by allowing them to share in these resources.
For example the discovery of the so-called manganese nodules in the deep seabed, which are usually found thousands of metres deep and far beyond the exclusive economic zones of any one country, will some day allow lesser developed countries to also benefit from this enormous potential for economic growth.
I am quite aware however that our own Canadian mining industry, most of it land based, feels threatened by this part of the agreement. That is because these manganese nodules consist of large deposits of nickel and copper.
I find it difficult to follow the logic of this argument. Experts agree that once the Law of the Sea is ratified Canada will rank in the top five countries to gain sovereign control over more surface area and undersea territory.
Considering the enormous pressure placed on countries in the southern hemisphere to play economic catch up with the north to avoid a massive debt crisis and so on, it only makes sense to adopt a share approach to resource management. The Law of the Sea Convention would therefore serve as an invaluable and efficient instrument to facilitate ocean development.
Remember that we are talking about sharing, not giving away, precious resources.
Consider the economic cost of delaying the development of these types of mineral resources. Why tangle with the World Court in an unending series of resource disputes when the alternative is a rational and fair approach to ocean resource management?
The third major principle of the Law of the Sea pertains to the preservation of the seas and the rights of other states. With certain rights come certain obligations. Consider drift-net fishing and what can be described as nothing less than the wholesale rape of the high seas.
In addition to outlining the rights of states to fish, mine and navigate the sea we must also accept certain obligations to preserve and protect the ocean for future generations. Indeed the International Law of the Sea represents a constitution for the oceans, a means of establishing an international order above and below the sea.
I think the Law of the Sea should be an integral component of the new world order that the international community is talking about. Right now all the G-7 members, the most highly developed economies in the world, are refusing to ratify this treaty. Sadly this government has placed Canada among those nations that are refusing to ratify.
Now I know the game. This Prime Minister and this government are afraid to show leadership. They follow. They are waiting to see what the other G-7 countries will do. In international politics Canada should show leadership. Canada should be the first of the G-7 countries to sign this treaty. If Canada does that I think the other six
