countries will sign right after. If that happens then this on the high seas is increasingly recognized as an intema-Law the of the Sea does become the law of the oceans, tional environmental issue.
It is time to take a leadership role and show the rest of the world that Canada is no longer the chicken of the sea. For the sake of present and future generations I encourage all members to support this motion. To the people listening to this debate, phone the member for Davenport and get a copy of this motion because it is so vital. I cannot stress this enough. When we talk about the new world order, this is part of it. This should be an integral component.
I congratulate the hon. member for Davenport for always looking into the future, protecting our planet not for ourselves but for future generations. Congratulations.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again we are debating the motion brought forward by the hon. member for Davenport which states:
That, in the opinion of the House, the government should, for the benefit of Canadian fisheries, urgently take the necessary steps to ratify the International Law of the Sea, and urge other nations to do so in order to reach the 60 signatures required for the Law of the Sea to come into force.
The issue of the ratification of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, commonly referred to as UNCLOS, has been reviewed exhaustively in the previous two hours of debate in this House, on June 23 and December 3 of last year. It has also featured prominently on two other occasions: an opposition day debate on foreign overfishing on March 12 of last year and a special debate on May 7, 1992 on the UNCED which referred extensively to our legal initiative on high-seas fisheries at UNCED in Rio.
During these debates it has been repeatedly demonstrated that this motion subscribes to a simple but wholly ineffective solution to the crisis facing the Canadian Atlantic fishery.
The government's approach to the problem of foreign overfishing has been to seek a solution through practical measures of international co-operation. Ratification of UNCLOS at this time would do nothing in terms of practical results to resolve the overfishing issue. However slowly, significant progress is being made. Overfishing
In terms of control of fisheries resources, Canada already benefits from one of the most significant provisions of UNCLOS. That is the creation of the 200-mile exclusive economic zone, since this now forms part of customary international law. Indeed the foreign overfishing problem is related to fishing beyond the 200-mile limit so Canada would not enhance its control over this problem whether or not it ratifies the UNCLOS.
Further, it is widely known that the long-standing difficulties within the international community with regard to UNCLOS ratification concern not the control of fisheries resources but the seabed mining provisions. All industrialized countries except Iceland have serious concerns in this regard. Ratification by Canada at this time could well commit the Canadian Treasury to disproportionate financial obligations to the UN authority responsible for the exploitation of deep seabed resources.
Canada is actively engaged in the informal consultations with the Secretary General of the United Nations. It is carrying this out in order to resolve the problems concerning the exploration and the exploitation of these resources.
I would like to talk in terms of the fisheries and what has been done on that situation. Since the House last discussed the issue in early December, we have made important strides in the direction of solving the fishing problems.
Let us talk about the Law of the Sea. Protect our fisheries.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
If the hon. member opposite will just pay attention we will get to these points. First, the fisheries agreement with the European Community was initialled on December 17 and provides for adherence to the conservation decisions of the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization, better known as NAFO.
Second, as a result of consultations with contracting parties to NAFO Morocco and Venezuela have agreed to withdraw their vessels from the NAFO regulatory area. Panama has fined several of its vessels fishing in that area and de-registered two. We have also recently held

Private Members' Business
consultations with Korea in which we urged that country to withdraw its vessels from the NAFO area.
Third, on December 22 the United Nations General Assembly adopted resolutions 47/192, formally convening the United Nations conference in straddling fish stocks and highly migratory fish stocks.
This conference will provide for the first time a forum to develop rules for the management of high seas fisheries in accordance with conservation and sustainable development principles within the framework for international co-operation established by UNCLOS. It will also continue to focus international attention on overfishing on the high seas, thereby increasing the pressure to stop this practice.
The conference will start its substantive work with a three-week session in July in New York after a five-day organizational session in April. It aims to complete its work before the 49th session of the General Assembly in the fall of 1994.
Canada is hoping that all countries with an interest in the sustainability of high-seas fisheries will participate in the conference and support a substantive outcome that gives concrete expression to the rights, obligations and responsibilities of states to conserve the living resources on the high seas.
Fourth, to begin to prepare the ground for a successful outcome at the UN conference Canada hosted a meeting of like-minded countries on high-seas fisheries in St. John's, Newfoundland from January 21 to 24. Over 50 countries attended this meeting, including Argentina, Australia, Chile, Iceland, Mexico, New Zealand, Russia and the United States, just to name a few of them.
The meeting focused on four discussion papers. There were three developed by Canada and one by New Zealand. As well, there was a comprehensive report on straddling stocks and highly migratory species, problems being experienced in various parts of the world.
The discussion papers dealt with the following subjects: (a) management principles for the conservation of straddling and highly migratory fish stocks on the high seas; (b) problems related to fisheries by states that are not members of the relevant regional conservation organizations or are new members thereof; (c) surveillance, control and enforcement on the high seas; (d) remedies; and lastly, (e) special problems of developing countries.
There was a consensus on the need for action on all elements addressed in the discussion papers. There was also a shared view that the UN conference must result in an effective regime of conservation and management for straddling stocks and highly migratory species.
By effective it was clear that participants at the meeting meant a regime that works in practice. Workability must be the essential criterion. Nothing less will do. This will require a political commitment on behalf of all states, including the distant water fishing states, to achieve solutions through the UN conference.
Fifth, Canada participated actively in an ad hoc informal group of experts which met from February 1 to 5 in Rome under the auspices of the Food and Agriculture Organization, FAO, to draft an agreement on the reflagging of fishing vessels to avoid compliance with internationally agreed conservation and management measures.
The group managed to agree on a very wide-ranging document which deals not only with the reflagging of fishing vessels but also with their initial flagging and with fishing by vessels flying the flag of states that are not members of relevant regional fisheries conservation organizations. The draft agreement would commit states accepting it to ensure that vessels flying their flag do not undermine internationally agreed conservation and management measures.
Deterrents provided by the draft agreement include mandatory registration of fishing vessels, their licensing to fish on the high seas on condition that they do not undermine internationally agreed conservation and management measures, and inspection and control by flagging in and flagging out states to avoid double flagging and changes of flag to undermine such measures.
There are enforcements by both categories of states, including penalties commensurate with the gravity of the offences, and hopefully an electronic information system centred in FAO but radiating to all parties to the agreement covering registered and licensed fishing vessels, those sighted committing infractions and the penalties imposed.
March 9, 1993

The member states of FAO will be seized of this draft agreement in the framework of its committee on fisheries which meets in Rome from March 15 to 19. If it commands a consensus the agreement will then be approved by the council in June and adopted by the FAO conference in November. Such a procedure would correspond to the fast-track approach that Canada has been pushing for.
While the results of the discussions in New York, St. John's and Rome which I have just described allow for a measure of optimism it is clear that over the long term much work remains to be done to make the most of the opportunities that have now arisen. These opportunities did not just happen by themselves. They were the result of hard work and singular dedication on the part of men and women in several coastal states, including Canada, who took on the responsibility of putting high seas overfishing on the international agenda.
I hope I have made it clear that, as is all too frequently the case, the opposition has seized on ratification of the Law of the Sea Convention as a simple solution to a very complex problem. Passage of this motion by the House would in effect endorse a facile gesture easily implemented but completely ineffective and potentially costly which would do nothing to alleviate the real problem of overfishing in the high seas.
I trust that the defeat of this motion will reinforce our common commitment to resolve serious crises facing the Canadian fishery by effective means and not through empty rhetoric.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise in support of the motion of the hon. member for Davenport this afternoon.
I would like to draw to the attention of the House how timely this debate is in light of The Fifth Estate on March 2 exposing the gross practice of drift-net fishing off the Pacific coast and the complete abdication of governmental responsibility in addressing this problem.
The ratification of the Law of the Sea is only one step because it takes more than just signatures on a document. It takes government priorities and resources to enforce what is intended in the Law of the Sea. I see neither from this government.
Private Members' Business
It is very curious. Last summer in my province, when close to 500,000 sockeye salmon went missing from the Fraser River during implementation of the aboriginal fishing plan, a fish war erupted. Commercial and native groups were at each other's throats. Ottawa ordered an investigation by Professor Peter Pearse and the House of Commons fisheries committee conducted its own hearings.
However, when an offshore foreign drift-net fleet- those curtains of death that do not just take B.C. salmon but take everything-routinely takes between 250,000 to
500,000	B.C. salmon per year Ottawa says it is not a major problem and represents only .5 per cent of the total stocks. This does little to inspire confidence that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans is considering the $500 million salmon industry in British Columbia.

Ratifying this Law of the Sea Convention is a minimum. It must be ratified. Then there are the enforcement and surveillance provisions to protect our salmon stocks, for which our tax dollars have funded enhancement programs. Our salmon stocks provide processing jobs, provide food fishery for native people and commercial fishery people, and a livelihood for both native and non-native people.
One becomes suspect at what the motivation of the government is in allotting so many resources to find
500,000	salmon in the Fraser River that had gone missing and yet alloting no resources when a drift-net fleet comes and takes our resource.
The Law of the Sea has been ratified by 56 nations. It only requires four more nations to ratify it before it becomes international law. I do not understand this government dragging its feet on this. Consider the cost to the Treasury in not ratifying this. It is just nonsensical. It is a $500 million B.C. salmon industry. There is no surveillance. The undercover unit from fisheries and

oceans has been disbanded and our resource is now being processed in Thailand.
A constituent of mine phoned me late last week in response to a stoiy on The Fifth Estate. He said that he had notified fisheries and oceans three years ago that Canadian salmon was being sold in Germany in product of Canada tins, but was obviously canned in Thailand. Mr. Speaker, just a few words in support of this motion by the hon. member for Davenport.
It is amazing, is it not, when we realize that there is no Law of the Sea. Every time we listen to an official of fisheries and oceans or of external affairs or a cabinet minister talking about the fishery, reference is made to the Law of the Sea. Well, there is no Law of the Sea. The Law of the Sea right now at this very moment is made up by a group of nations that want to catch fish or want to exploit a resource. In support of the hon. member for Davenport and what he is trying to do, let me point this out to the House and to the Canadian people.
After the Canadian fishing industry on the east coast had closed down fish plants and told fishermen to go home and stay there, 1993 opened with 14 factory vessels from Japan, licensed by the Canadian government, fishing 75 miles from the shore of Nova Scotia.

sitting home and cannot get tuna licences. That is reality. That is the Law of the Sea today. There is nothing about conservation at all. The bluefin tuna is an endangered species today because of that. With all of the Canadian fish plants closed, workers are sitting at home and are getting a cheque from the government. On November 27, 1992, while those fishermen were getting a cheque for sitting at home in the province of Newfoundland, there was a Russian boat 50 miles from St. John's, Newfoundland, catching redfish after we closed down a redfish plant. Why? That is the law of the sea. That is the law according to the Department of External Affairs and the latest meeting it had in some fancy meeting hall in some capital across the ocean.
The Department of Fisheries and Oceans has evidence of massive dumping at sea this year, last year, the year before and the year before that because of the technology used by foreign vessels both inside our 200-mile zone and outside our 200-mile zone. Fisheries and oceans has evidence from the observers-because I have it-that shows 10 tonnes of fish dumped with practically every haul-back. When the gigantic nets are hauled over the side of the boat they are filled too much to get through the opening. The Department of Fisheries and Oceans has the evidence of that year after year after year and even last year. That is the incredible thing. They have the technology to do it. We do not have that technology. We do not have one factory freezer trawler in Canada, not one single factory freezer trawler and we do not want one.
There are 104 observers employed in St. John's, Newfoundland, there are 85 employed in Halifax, Nova Scotia, and there are a dozen in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. What are their jobs? Their jobs are to observe aboard a foreign vessel licensed by Ottawa, and the foreign vessel is a factory freezer trawler. There are 104 jobs in St. John's, 85 in Halifax and a dozen in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. They are observing aboard factory freezer trawlers with a technology that destroys every last thing in the ocean inside the 200-mile zone and outside the 200-mile zone. That is the law of the sea today.
The law of the sea today is that Canadian fishermen will sit at home because the Canadian government will not sign the Law of the Sea treaty that will put an end to dumping and put an end to this business of fishing on every spawning ground in the world. We have it in the observer reports at the Department of Fisheries and Oceans today on 200 Kent Street on the tenth floor in a locked compartment. Mr. Speaker, since no one else wishes to speak I am very happy to be able to take the floor.

It is very sad that we could not hear from the member for Surrey-White Rock-South Langley on what he thinks about the Law of the Sea and whether he has any input to this debate because what we are discussing here today is of course the convention called the Law of the Sea. We are also discussing here today Canada's reputation in the world.
Canada was a pioneer in the time preceding the coming to life of this convention. Canada was among the nations that pushed very hard in the formulation of the contents of this document that finally saw the light of day in 1982. It was the brain-child of former Ambassador Beesley and it received substantial political support from the Canadian government at the time.
The step of signing it was taken by the Government of Canada very shortly after. Canada was one of the nations that signed this document immediately after it was introduced. We were among the first to launch it.
We come to the second step. A convention needs two steps. The first is the signature and the second is its ratification. Now that we are in the ratification stage we find Canada lagging, dragging its feet, and using arguments of the kind that we heard from the parliamentary secretary earlier.
We probably share the longest coastal area of all nations in the world. We are probably ahead of Australia. While we drag our feet as a nation other nations have gradually ratified it. It has now reached the point where 56 nations have ratified it. The world community is only four ratifications short of the convention coming into effect. We are that close. At this rate it looks very likely, unless the government changes its mind, that Canada will not be among the first 60 nations ratifying it or launching it. It is very sad.
Today we heard the parliamentary secretary talking in his speech about this measure as an ineffective solution. That is what he said in his speech half an hour ago. The parliamentary secretary was contradicting the Minister
of Fisheries and Oceans who said on May 5 in Cancun on Canada's behalf: "The Law of the Sea outlines principles and measures that will give proper effect to the provision of the Law of the Sea Convention". The minister was representing Canada when he said that, and today the parliamentary secretary said that the law would be ineffective.
One wonders who prepared the speech. What is going on in the ranks of the government if a parliamentary secretary contradicts a public statement made internationally on the same convention only six months ago? What has happened in the thought processes of the government since May of last year? One wonders. Has it turned around? Obviously not. At least one would hope it has not gone bananas.
Three very strong aspects of the convention must be stressed again. First, by ratifying the convention Canada would ensure that high sea fisheries would pursue ecologically sound practices. Second, the convention would ensure a much better degree of maintenance of the ecology of the marine system in the oceans.
The member for Gander-Grand Falls referred to sections 63 and 64. It is all there for us to read. It is as simple as that. It is black on white. It is unbelievable the government would have the gall to say that this convention would be an ineffective solution.
Third, the convention would complete the protection of fish stocks within the 200-mile exclusive economic zone and probably permit us to manage better the straddling stocks, as others have already said.
One wonders conceptually what is standing in the way of the thought processes of this government. One can only suspect that there are very strong mining interests and that pressures have been exerted on the Government of Canada, and I suspect on the United States, by large multinationals such as Inco, Noranda and others urging that the convention not be ratified.
There are substantial interests related to seabed resources. For the life of me I cannot understand why sectoral interests must stand in the way of an overwhelming and all-embracing interest in the fish wealth of oceans which touches so closely the livelihood of many communities. We are talking of hundreds of thousands
March 9, 1993

of families and communities whose livelihood depends on fish.
Therefore the convention as such is much more than just introducing strong international law that is badly needed. It is a social and economic instrument of the first order. It is perhaps for the first time the international community coming together and saying that we must jointly manage our fish resources, properly. I suspect the reason for requiring 60 signatory nations to ratify this convention was to develop sufficient momentum, sufficient political will, and it is being developed.
This is a tragedy for Canada. We are not seizing the opportunity. We do not see meaning or the opportunity for Canada in ratifying it. All we can say is that we are using portions of the Law of the Sea that are convenient to us but we will not sign it because the Treasury Board finds it too expensive. This is the logic that we heard today and in preceding debates.
In other words we want to pick and chose. We want to do it where it is convenient for us but we do not want to carry the burden. Probably until now this government has subordinated Canada's fisheries interest to the interests that are being lobbied in Washington and in other capitals by the mining sector.
Canada cannot pick and chose. Canada must join the world community and ratify the convention sooner or later. It was our hope in the opposition that we could draw the government to do it sooner rather than later for the sake of our own reputation, for the sake of our own credibility.
There will be a preparatory conference in New York next April on the question of fisheries. There will be a full-fledged conference in July flowing from UNCED, the United Nations Conference on the Environment and Development. How we can go there without having ratified the convention and having credibility I do not know.

Mr. Speaker, it is rather tough to speak on an issue as important as breast implants with people leaving the House and all of the distractions.
The minister announced on January 13 of this year what most considered would be a ban on the further use of silicone breast implants. He announced that manufacturing would no longer take place and he notified the manufacturers that they would have to have valid notices of compliance for the sale of implants. Only with additional information will the department consider the reintroduction of implants. Is this really the case?
The minister also said that only in exceptional circumstances will women have access to silicone implants and only then on compassionate grounds. What guidelines will be used to determine compassionate? Will it be the persuasive words of the surgeon or the lobbying efforts of the manufacturers?
It should be noted that under the current regulations, physicians are allowed to request silicone implants on a case by case basis. It will be up to the department to determine the merits of the application of the doctor. Again one must ask: What guidelines is the minister using to determine the merits of the application? On what grounds will these applications be judged?
What we seem to have now is not a ban, but just one more bureaucratic hurdle for plastic surgeons to pass before they can use these silicone breast implants.
On January 13 the minister introduced his moratorium or ban on silicone implants. On January 15 in Montreal, within two days of the minister's announcement, the

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to put one or two pieces of information on the record with respect to the question which has just been raised by my hon. friend.
First of all, as many Canadians know, the proposal for the fixed link was put to an environmental assessment. Public hearings were held and the panel, when it reported, established criteria under which such a proposal would indeed be acceptable.
The panel was very concerned about the adverse affects which lingering ice would have on the environment and it was with that criteria in mind that the Minister of Public Works undertook his responsibilities to publish first of all the government's response to the panel and then to examine the feasibility of the fixed link thereafter.
As my hon. friend has just said, in January 1991 the government appointed an independent committee of ice experts to examine the effects of the bridge on the departure of spring ice. That group concluded that it would be possible to build a bridge across the strait that would meet the panel's ice-out requirements, as they are called.
I want to stress that there has been public participation in this process. It is an ongoing process. The government and the Minister of Public Works are very committed to ensuring that our obligations under section 33(c) and (d) of the Environmental Assessment Review Process guidelines are met. In addition, the matter is also before the courts and so perhaps any further comment on my part should be left to a later time.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to continue an argument I have had with this government dating back to my first election about economic renewal and economic support for Manitoba.
My specific question arose from a conflict between the premier of Manitoba, the finance minister and the Prime Minister over the support provided by the federal government to the city of Winnipeg.
While it is not my job to defend the actions of the Government of Manitoba I thought that the incident indicated the degree to which Manitobans are frustrated by this federal government and the degree to which they would like to see a more co-operative attitude.
Starting over a decade ago Winnipeg was supported through a core area initiative. Subsequent to the signing of the second accord by this government there were many promises made that there would be a third accord. That has not taken place. Instead we have had a gradual decline in the quality of life and not only in the inner city. Poverty has spread into many older neighbourhoods throughout Winnipeg. Of course the plague of rural Manitoba is well known to anybody who follows the plight of rural Canada.
We keep asking the government these questions because there are things that can be done. There is a need for an economic plan, one of which touches upon the transportation needs of Winnipeg. It should address the international role that could be played by the airport and support for the rail system, the branch lines, making sure that if the two major companies withdraw from the branch lines across western Canada that we have an infrastructure left for someone else.
We have to deal with the port of Churchill which has a very proper role to be played in trade with northern Europe. We have to deal with the questions of research and development in Winnipeg, not only in the health industry but in other industries as well. We have to deal with the question of the cultural industries which on their own in a very lonely fashion produce some of the best works in North America, if not in the world. In fact the Winnipeg film group is world famous for some of its work.
Adjournment Debate
These need the support of the federal government. As cutbacks go from one department to the other for reasons which members from Manitoba simply cannot understand, this province continues to be singled out: transfer payments, support for post-secondary education, support for health care, support for job training, support for aboriginal economic development, support for inner city businesses, support for new immigrants who are looking for English as a second language training. The list is lengthy.
The response of the government when asked a question in Question Period or response in debate is not to respond in a positive way, to pick up the phone and say we know your frustrations, we are trying to figure out what to do, this is the blockage, can you help. When you talk about partnerships in government you do not isolate people who are genuinely concerned about these issues. You try to find a way to get them involved. It does not have to be for public consumption but it can be just to see something happen.
Many groups from the inner cities come to me and say: "We do not want a public confrontation with the minister. We want someone to go to the minister to ask under what grounds he will solve this problem so that we understand what is going on".
The constant failure of the government to reach out to Winnipegers has caused a political alienation that will take years to recover from and years to reform. I continue this debate with the government because it is very important that a new government be formed which responds to the economic needs of Winnipegers.
